They lived in close association with the sea, which surrounded them on three sides. Therefore, it is not surprising that many of their traditional stories feature sea animals.

The two young men thought about it and then one of them spoke up and said, "We will go home."  And so they took their guns and went home.  The people on the other side of the river were very pleased with themselves, and they said, "Now we are the only people who can hunt seals, because the two-legged people have gone home." They had long, flat faces and necks, and big noses.  Their eyes were slanted and their bodies were skinny.  They weren't bad people, they just looked funny."

The story
Once upon a time there were two young men from the Inuit village of Egigalik (Egulac) near the modern dayettlement of Pangnirtung, Nunavut, Canada. They were out on the fjord one night hunting seals when suddenly it grew foggy and calm. As the men were far from the village, they were not expecting any help to come. However, as they were hunting on the men's territory, the people from the village came out and began shouting, "Kunuja! Kunuja!" which means "Come back! Come back!" They were afraid that the young men would drown in the river and so they continued shouting until the men returned to the safety of the shore. When the two hunters finally made it back, the people of the village gave them feasts and celebrated because they were grateful that the men had come back to them.

The village worked together to bring the men back to safety, demonstrating the power of community. Additionally, the story shows the negative consequences of individualistic actions. Background
This is one of several similar tales collected by Frank Speck in 1908–1910 in the Kootenay region of southeastern British Columbia. It is an example of a "tale of friendship" found in the speech of the Ktunaxa people. In this genre, two friends go on a hunting or fishing trip, where they engage in an activity that results in one of them getting killed. This type of story is found among many Native American groups. The similarity of the stories shows that the peoples of the Columbia River basin had strong similarities in their material culture and social relationships.These stories were collected by Frank Speck in 1908–1910 as part of the George M. Wrinkle expedition. Wrinkle was a self-proclaimed "anthropologist" who sought to collect Native American material culture and oral traditions. He assembled a team of field workers to visit various Native American groups in the interior of British Columbia, including  Somerset Parker, Frank Speck, and Edward A. Mootta. The expedition was funded by the Anthropological Society of London and the Royal Anthropological Institute of Great Britain and Ireland. The journey was undertaken in two phases. In the first phase, the group collected artifacts and specimens without any particular systematic plan. In the second phase, the group systematically collected oral traditions, myths, and folklore. History
The tale is a Native American folktale, originally told by the Nlaka'pamux, Salish, and Shuswap peoples of the interior of southwestern British Columbia. The tale was recorded by Marius Bear, a B.C. provincial cultural consultant, in 1978. Bear claimed that the tale was told to him by a man named Frank Arthur, who said that it was a story told to him by his grandfather, who was a trapper.

Analysis
The tale is a membership tale, in which the members of a group (in this case, young men who hunt seals) are killed by outsiders, and the survival of the group is threatened. The tale also contains a morbid element, as the two men are left out in the wilderness to die. Although the tale is classified as a folktale, it contains elements of reality, as hunting accidents do occur. The tale may have originated as a warning to young men to be aware of their surroundings and to be careful when hunting.

Variations
A variation of this tale is told by the Lilloet as "The Two Boys and the Seal Hunters". In this version, two boys are out hunting for salmon with their father, and they spot a group of seal hunters on the other side of the river. The father tells the boys to hide and not disturb the seal hunters, but the boys ignore their father's warning and start shouting and laughing. The seal hunters from across the river become angry and come over to the side of the two boys and kill them.

The story is a traditional Inuit legend. It was recorded by Richard Finch in 1941 while he was working as a teacher in the settlement of Egulac (nicknamed "Eskimo Point") on the west coast of Hudson Bay. Finch recorded many traditional Inuit stories and songs during his 25 years as a teacher in Eskimo Point. This particular story was told to Finch by a man named Emanuel Jangles.
Finch wrote that this story was told by Eskimo elders to help explain certain natural phenomena, in this case, the fog that frequently rolls in off the ocean.  According to Finch, the story was also told to provide an explanation for the importance of community and the dangers of isolating yourself from others.

This story comes from the people of the Northwest Coast of Oregon and is part of the Nagoda cycle of stories.  It was recorded by Edward S. Curtis in 1909.

This story appears to be a cautionary tale about going out onto the river in a canoe without taking proper precautions. The story of "The Two Young Men" is an example of a transformational myth.  In this story, the two young men are transformed into seals and then back into humans.  This type of myth is common in many indigenous cultures and can be seen in the stories of "The Boy Who Turned Into a Bear" and "The Girl Who Became a Swan".  These stories often teach listeners about the interconnectedness of all living things and the importance of sharing and community.  In "The Two Young Men", the men learn about the importance of giving to the community  and then subsequently are given a task to perform for the community.  After they are transformed back into humans, they continue to act out the role of the seals and thus maintain the balance of the ecosystem.

The legend does not indicate that either side fully understood the other, but communication was able to prevent a fight.

The people from the village went back to the river the next day to look for the two men, but they had disappeared.  The people were worried and puzzled about the disappearance of the two men, and they stayed worried and puzzled for a long time.  Eventually they decided that the men must have been kidnapped by evil spirits and they held a ceremony to try to get the men back.  But the men did not return, and everyone was sad.  Eventually they forgot about the two men and went back to their normal lives, although the memory of the event stayed with some of the older people.

Analysis
This story is a good example of how the people from different cultures can interpret the same events differently.  In this story, the people from Egulac thought that the torches were attackers coming to kill them, and the people from the village thought that the Egulac men had been kidnapped by evil spirits.  These different interpretations led to the Egulac men not returning, which probably caused more confusion and worry for the people involved.  Eventually, the people from both villages were able to go back to their normal lives, although the memory of the event stayed with some of the older people.

Analyses
In some Eskimo stories, there is a character who transformation can change between human and seal. In this story, the seal man is a being who can transform into a human, but is usually in his seal form. He is considered a dangerous and evil being who tries to trick and kill humans. In this story, the heroic young men are able to fool the seal man and protect their village.
Unlike most Eskimo stories, this one does not have a moral. Instead, it is a story that explains a traditional Eskimo activity, and how the people from the village were able to protect themselves from a being that meant them harm.

Traditional tale
The traditional version of this tale tells that it was not fog and calm that caused the young men to drown, but rather that they were lured into the water by a seal-woman who lived in the river. According to the tale, she came to the surface and sang a song, and the men were so enchanted by her song that they forgot all about the fog and the cold and jumped into the water to swim out to her. But when they got out to the seal-woman, she transformed herself into a monster, and the two men were drowned and their bodies found floating in the river the next morning.

Tale from the Nuu-chah-nulth people
This tale comes from the Nuu-chah-nulth people, also called the Numu or Neh-mew-teet, and is collected from Gabriel Hostie, a hereditary chief of the Tla-gul-si-am clan of the Yuaat village on Meekma Inlet, located north of Bella Coola on the west coast of Canada. It was recorded by Marianne Mills in 1996.

Analysis
This tale features many elements typical of Nuu-chah-nulth tales, including a supernatural being, an enchanted landscape, and the dangers of forgetting traditional teachings and ignoring warnings. It also shows the high value placed on human relationships and social order in Nuu-chah-nulth culture, as the two young men are warned not to hunt alone, but they go out anyway, and suffer the consequences.

It is an example of a genre of oral tradition known as "trickster tales," in which a culture's established social norms and expectations are subverted for comedic effect. In this tale, the Egulac people are depicted as outsiders to the village, presumably a group of itinerant hunters who occasionally passed through the area. The villagers express wariness and even hostility toward this group, presumably because of their uncertain status as members of the local community.

Boas did not feel it was proper to publication the names of the men involved. The tale was published by Boas in 1896 in the journal Science.

History
This tale has been told by the people of Saniku (also spelled "Egulac") on Prince of Wales Island, located north of Metlakatla, for more than 100 years. Analysis
This tale is an example of a vanishing culture tale. It shares motifs with other vanishing culture tales, such as "The House of the Scorched-Face Woman", in which ignorant outsiders bring disease and destruction to a formerly isolated people. In this tale, the outsiders are not literally women, but rather represent outsiders to the Saniku people. The tale may have been invented to explain the arrival of disease and other destructive technologies to the Saniku people. The tale is also an example of a cautionary tale. The two young men ignore the advice of their elders and pay the ultimate price.

Analysis
This legend clearly shows the fear that the people of that time held for the sea and the inability of humans to control the forces of nature. The fog, which is a natural phenomenon, is personified as a being that can swallow up two men, thus demonstrating the supernatural elements that were attributed to cause natural phenomena. The people from the village attempt to exert control over the situation by calling out to the hunters to come home, but since they are unable to hear the calls, the hunters are regarded as having been swallowed by the fog, and thus lost. The legendary hero, Nawozo, who is said to have been swallowed by the sea, also demonstrates the fear of the people of that time for the sea.

Then the people from the village came out and saw that there was no light and they could not see where they were going, and they had to turn back. But the two young men continued hunting and they caught seven seals. When they had finished hunting they made a big fire and they sat by the fire and they sang songs. Then the people from the village came back and they saw the fire and they knew that the young men were there. So they went to the edge of the sea and called out to the young men to come back to the village. But the young men did not come back and the people were very angry with the young men and they did not speak to them for a long time.
 Then the elders of the village called a meeting and they said that they must go out and bring back the young men or they would all starve because there was no food.  They went out and they found the young men and they brought them back to the village and they were very happy to see them. From that time on the young men went out hunting every night and brought back food to the village and they were happy.

Analysis
This story reflects the importance of community and cooperation in Inuit culture. Hunting is an essential activity for survival in the harsh climate of the Arctic, and the community relies on the success of hunters. The story also demonstrates the respect for elders and the importance of traditions. The anger of the community towards the young men reflects the seriousness of hunting for food and the responsibility that comes with it.

Then the people from the village came down to the river to swim and play and the two young men from Egulac had to swim back to the village without catching any seals.  They were cold and tired from swimming, so they asked for permission to rest on the shore for a while.  The people from the village said they could, but they were afraid that the young men would take advantage of them and steal their wives and daughters.  So, the people from the village swam out to the middle of the river and brought back a seal for each of the young men from Egulac as a gift to show they were not going to steal any wives or daughters.

The story is part of the oral tradition of the Tlingit people of Alaska.  It was recorded by Father John Daly, a Jesuit missionary who lived among the Tlingit in 1880.  In the story, Egulac refers to the Tlingit village where the two young men came from.  The story is also found in a book by William Reid, entitled "Tlingit Myths and Legends".  In Reid's version, the two young men are named Kudach and Kyudya.  In both versions, the story is told as a myth.  It is classed as a myth because the Tlingit people themselves classify their oral traditions into three categories:  stories, history, and magic.  This story is a story.

Analysis
The story of the Two Young Men from Egulac is a type of origin story.  It explains where the Tlingit people got their land and what the rules are for sharing women.  The story also shows some of the attitudes that the Tlingit people have towards women.  Women are seen as a precious resource that must be protected.  They are also seen as a cause of war.  In this story, if the two young men had taken wives from the village, war would have resulted.

Then the people from the village came down to the river to swim and play in the fog and calm.  As the young men were swimming out to sea, one of them knocked over a post marking the edge of the fishing ground and the other one pulled down the rope attached to the post.  There was a sudden loud knock on the side of the canoe.  Both young men were terrified and paddled back to the village as fast as they could.  When they got there, they told the villagers about their experience and how they had almost been caught by the monster living underwater at the edge of the fishing grounds.  From that time on, the people of Egulac respected the sea and the monster and never fished those waters again.

Retelling
Once upon a time there was a village called Egulac. Two young men from this village went down to the river one night to hunt seals. It was a still night with fog and calm winds. As they were swimming out to sea from the river, one of them knocked over a post that marked the boundary of the fishing ground and the other one pulled down the rope attached to the post. Just then there was a loud knock on the side of their canoe, which made the two young men terrified. They quickly paddled back to the village as fast as they could. When they got there, they told the other villagers about their experience and how they had almost been caught by the monster living underwater at the edge of the fishing grounds. From that time on, the people of Egulac respected the sea and the monster and never fished those waters again.

Analysis
This legend tells us that there are boundaries which human beings should not cross, and if we do we might face dangerous consequences. In this legend, the two young men were fishing in an area which they were not permitted to fish in and as a result, they almost lost their lives. Similarly, in many Indigenous communities, there are stories about the consequences of crossing boundaries

Then the people from the village came out to hunt and they got all the seal they wanted. When the two young men went home they divided the prey. One took the best part of the catch and ate it. The other took the least desirable part and threw it away. Later the one who had taken the best part of the catch grew rich, while the one who had taken the least desirable part grew poor. This story illustrates the negative consequences of selfishness and greed. It also demonstrates the importance of sharing and being satisfied with what one has.

Analysis
This tale is a member of the "Greedy man gets none" subtype of the larger "Gift" theme found in many Indigenous stories.  It is similar to tales such as "The Girl Who Bought a Century" and "The Water Creation Myth."  In these stories, a character is given a gift, but instead of being satisfied with the gift, they insist on getting more.  In the case of "The Two Young Men from Egulac," the protagonist not only keeps for himself the best part of the seal he has hunted, but he then discards the remainder of his catch.  This selfishness causes him to lose out on future hunts and cause hardship for his family.  Conversely, the tale rewards the protagonist who shares his catch and is satisfied with what he has.The negative consequences of the protagonist's greed are not immediate.  He is initially rewarded for his actions, receiving "the best part of the catch."  However, as the tale makes clear, this initial reward is a result of luck rather than any intrinsic value he has earned.  Because of his greed, he then fails to participate in future hunts, resulting in the family going without meat.  This shows that the tale is not merely a cautionary tale about the dangers of greed, but also one that promotes the importance of community and the cyclical nature of resources.

Analysis
This is another example of a story in which the primary conflict arises from the interaction of the protagonist with other members of his community.  In this story, the conflict appears to be purely social, arising from the fear and disapproval of the narrator's community for the protagonist's activity.  It is not clear what specific action the two young men took which caused the villagers to react with fear and disapproval, although the reference to their hunting seals in the river suggests that they may have been violating tribal taboos or traditions.  The story does not provide enough information to determine whether the conflict is ultimately resolvable.

Then all of a sudden, a big seal jumped up on the bank beside them and one of the young men saw it and shouted, "There's a seal!" The other young man replied, "I see it! Let's go home!" So they went home and the one who had seen the seal told his father and brothers and they went to the river to hunt seals but they caught nothing.
They went back to the place where the young men had seen the seal and the young men said, "This is where we saw the seal, we must come back here." They kept going back to the place where the young men had seen the seal and they caught an abundance of food so they were happy.
One night while they were out on the land a man came to them in a dream and said, "The seal is not real. It is a test to see if you are strong enough to be a real hunter. If you keep coming back here you will starve and die." The young men went back to their village and forgot about seals.

Analysis
This legend is about a test that the gods set up for the people of Egulac to see if they were strong enough to be hunters. The test was to go out and hunt seals but it was a trick because there were no seals in the river. If the people of Egulac had kept going out to the river to hunt seals they would have probably starved and died. Therefore, the gods saved them from that fate by letting one of them see the seal so that they would know where to hunt and what kind of animal to hunt for. The legend shows the importance of animals in the lives of the people of Egulac and how they relied on the animals for their food.

Then the people from the other side of the river, from across the creek, came over to the side where the two young men were, and by mistake, some of them stepped into the water and some of them stayed on the shore. The people who stepped into the water all drowned, but the people who stayed on the shore survived.

Explanation
This legend is an example of a common Arctic story about people drowning in a river or a creek. It shows that even though the story has a simple form, it still has important elements of a story.  The important elements in this story are the setting, the conflict, and the consequence.
Settlements along the coast of the Arctic all had fishing and hunting as a major part of their economy. Seals were an important source of food. Hunting accidents happened frequently along the coast. This legend describes a hunting accident where two young men went seal hunting and got lost in the fog.
Conflict and consequence are the two most important elements in this legend. The conflict in this story is the fog that causes the two young men to get lost and mistake the other side of the river for their own. The consequence is that some of the people from each group drowned and some survived.
Another important element in this legend is the repeatable action. The story can be summarized in two repeatable actions: 1. Two young men went down to the river to hunt seals. 2. Some people from each group drowned and some survived.
This legend has been passed down through the oral tradition for a long time. It has been collected and re-told many times. This specific version was collected by Frank Dierenmacher from George Angutti.

Then the people from the village came down to the river to swim and play.  The young men had trouble seeing the people in the fog and accidentally hit one of the villagers with the butt of their rifle, killing him. The two men then had to decide whether to tell the village about what had happened or not. Adaptation
In Ernest J. Gaines's 1996 play, "The Blue Room", the story is adapted with the characters changed to Emanuel and Lummie, and the event occurring in 1968. The play is set in the fictitious Louisiana town of Mt. Pilgrim. The tale is told by Emanuel, who is sitting in a jail cell. He is waiting for the authorities to come and take him to trial. The crime he is accused of committing is the murder of a teenage boy named Leroy Jones. Emanuel admits to killing Leroy, but claims it was an accident. He says that he and his friend Lummie were out hunting and it was dark when they came across Leroy and his girlfriend, Kathleen. According to Emanuel, Kathleen was sitting on Leroy's lap, and as he was getting ready to propose to her, Emanuel accidentally discharged his gun and the bullet killed Leroy. In the play, Emanuel is thinking back to that night and how things could have been different if only he had not drunk so much.

Then the people from the village began to come out and watch them from the shore.  After a while, one of the young men raised his hand to call to the other that he had caught something, but the fog was so thick that he could not see his partner, and while he waited and called out he began to imagine all sorts of things.  He thought that his partner might have been captured by the ghost of the river, or that he might have been carried away by the current, or that he might have been attacked by a monster.  He was just beginning to think that maybe he had been dreaming when he heard a voice behind him say, "Give us your hand and come back to the village with me."  He turned around and saw not a monster or a ghost but a girl standing there with her hand extended.  The two young men returned to the village and married the two girls who had been waiting for them.  From then on the men of the village would sometimes hunt down by the river, just for the pleasure of it, and sometimes they would bring their brides with them and stay by the river and have parties.

Analysis
This story is probably one of the most widely known of the Eskimo stories.  It is told by almost all of the groups of people who speak an Eskimo language.  It is a classic example of a universal folktale theme, the theme of the vanishing bridegroom or the absent partner.  The fear of being abandoned by one's partner is a common theme in many cultures.  The fear of losing one's partner is illustrated by the hero's fear that he has been deserted by his partner, and his relief when he sees the girl who has been waiting for him.  The story also contains elements of the magic myth, with the girl's appearance out of the fog.  The story is also an example of a more general folktale theme, the theme of the reward for braveness or for going out and seeking

It was a sound like someone walking on a smooth surface in stocking feet.  The young men from Egulac walked along the shore until they came to a cave, and when they entered the cave they saw a young woman sitting in the middle of the room.  Her hair was like rotten wood and her eyes were like black pebbles.  She said, "I am a witch.  I live in this cave.  Every night I come out and I walk along the shore.  If you kill me, then tonight you will have good fortune."  The two young men from Egulac were afraid, and they turned and ran away from the cave.  They ran to the opening of the cave and threw stones at the witch.  But the witch laughed and said, "You think you can kill me with your stones?  Every time I am hit by a stone I become stronger and stronger.  You must kill me with fire."  The men ran back into the village and gathered sticks and logs and came back to the cave and set it on fire.  The witch came out and said, "I am invulnerable to stones, but I cannot resist fire."  She threw a spell to protect herself, but the logs and stones fell on her and she burned to death.  After that, the two young men from Egulac went back to the cave and took her bones.  They treated her bones with respect, for she had given them the power to kill her, and therefore they had been given the power to do anything they wanted to do.  They carried the bones back to their village and buried them in a secret place.  From that time on, the people from Egulac had good fortune.

Then the people from the other side of the river came over, thinking that they were enemies, and began to attack the two men from Egulac. One of the Egulac men, named Wawaree, was a mighty warrior and he fought bravely, but eventually he was killed. The other Egulac man, named Matairo, pretended to be dead and survived the attack.
After some time had passed, Matairo went looking for his friend Wawaree's body, but he couldn't find it, and he began to think that perhaps Wawaree had not died after all. He went back to the place where he had been attacked and he found that Wawaree's body had been moved to another place. He took Wawaree's body back to his home and gave it a proper burial.
From that time on, the people from Egulac were known as the Miwok, which means "the brave people" in their language.

The hunters were lucky and managed to catch seven seals. However, when they were finishing up and preparing to leave, one of them stumbled and dropped his rifle. Being unable to find the weapon in the dark, he called out to his partner, "Where is my rifle?" His partner replied, "It's in the river." Being unable to swim out to retrieve the rifle, the first hunter shot at the river, missing the rifle but accidentally killing the other hunter. Thus, he was left alone and had to make his way back to the tribe without his companion.

In the morning, when the first hunter returned to the scene where he had left his partner, he was surprised to find his rifle missing. He then remembered that he had shot the rifle into the river, but he had failed to notice that his partner was not with him. Going back to the tribe to report the death of his companion, the first hunter was accused of murdering his partner. Despite his protests of innocence, the first hunter was about to be executed for the murder, but just then the chief of the tribe returned from a trip out of the region and declared that he would make a final decision on the matter.
The chief took one look at the hunter and knew that he had not committed murder, because even though he had been foolish enough to lose a rifle, he could not have shot his partner and left him to die in the river. The chief then imposed a sentence of one year of hard labor on the first hunter, after which he would be allowed to return to the tribe and take his rightful place as a member of the society.
The two hunters in this story are representative of the basic human condition. Then the people from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals by torchlight, and when the hunt was over they carried the seals home. In the morning, when the sun rose and the fog lifted, the people saw that there were two young men in the boat, but they knew nothing about who they were. Then the men from the village decided to wait until the next moon night to hunt seals again. On that night they went down to the river with torches as before, but now they drew up alongside the boat in which the two unknown men were sitting, and began to shout and scream. Terrified, the two young men jumped into the water and swam away. The people from Egulac then brought their boats up to the shore, got out, and began to search for the seals. When they had finished hunting, they went back to the village, and when they came to the place where the two young men had been sitting in the boat, they found the pockets turned inside out, and they knew that the men had taken something from the boat. Then the people from Egulac began to search for the two young men, and they did not find them anywhere.

Analysis
This legend is told by the people of Nunatsiavut, formerly known as Labrador Inuit. It tells of two unnamed young men who go hunting seals one night in a fog, and are presumed to be killed by the people from Egulac when they are seen sitting in a boat with turned-out pockets. The legend shows that the Inuit people were not always recognized as distinct from other groups, and describes a situation in which two young men are assumed to be members of another group based on their physical appearance and the assumption that they are therefore not members of the speaker's group. The legend also shows that hunting was an important part of Inuit culture and that fear of being mistaken for an enemy prevented the men from identifying themselves.

Courage, a young man who was with them, suggested they should head back soon, but the two other men, Ignorance and Foolishness, refused and decided to sit and wait until they had caught enough seals to satisfy them. As they sat and waited, the fog grew thicker and the calm became a curse, for just then the ice under them gave way and all three fell into the water and drowned.

Background
This story comes from the Koyukon people of the Iñupiat.  It is part of a larger story about a man named Pakanna who goes on a journey to retrieve the bones of his father, and along the way he hears this story from the people of Egulac.

Analysis
This story illustrates the dangers of ignoring the advice of others and being stubborn.  Courage, represented by the character of the same name in the story, is a positive trait, but when taken to an extreme can become a negative.  Ignorance and Foolishness are negative traits that can lead to unnecessary risks and even death.  The story as a whole reminds the listeners not to be foolish and stubborn, and to pay heed to the words and advice of others.

Then the people from the village began calling out in fear, "Beware! The two-headed monster is coming!"  The hunters ignored their warnings and continued hunting.  Suddenly, a monster with two heads came out of the water and grabbed one of the hunters.  It then disappeared back into the water.  The other hunter ran back to the village and told the people what had happened.  The people then decided to move to another location.  After the monster had been gone for a while, the hunters went back to the river to hunt seals but they were unsuccessful because the monster had come back.  Eventually, the monster was killed and it was discovered that it had two heads because one of its parents had been a monster and the other was a normal seal.  After that, the monster was no longer a threat and the hunters were able to hunt seals safely.

Analysis
"One Night Two Young Men from Egulac Went Down to the River to Hunt Seals" is a tale from the Kwakiutl people of the Northwest Coast of North America.  It involves a monster that is described as having two heads.  The monster is perceived as a threat to the safety of the hunters and the people of the village, causing them to move to another location.  It is eventually killed, ending its threat, and allowing the hunters to safely hunt seals once more.
The tale has been analyzed as an example of a type of legend known as a "monster legend".  Monster legends involve supernatural beings that are dangerous and must be overcome or avoided.  In this legend, the monster is described as having two heads, which is likely a metaphor for the danger and complexity of the monster.  The monster is said to have been born from the mating of a normal seal and a monster, giving it both good and evil traits.  This legend, like many others, teaches a moral about avoiding danger and respecting the natural world.

Then the people from the other side of the river, from over the mountains, came down to the river to hunt birds.  The young men did not see each other, and both sides thought the other was magical.  Eventually some people from Egulac went over to the other side of the river and they saw that the people over there were just ordinary people like themselves, and from then on they were friends.  This is the story of how the people from what is now called Kluane gained their name, and how the people from what is now called Tagish came to be called Tagish.  Both of these groups are tribes of the Tlingit people.
The story has different versions depending on who tells it.  Sometimes the two young men are porcupine hunters instead of seal hunters.  Sometimes the fog and calm come before the people from over the mountains come down to the river.  Sometimes the people from Egulac go over to the other side of the river first, and then the people from over the mountains come down to the river.  Sometimes the story is told with no reference to tlingit people at all.

This story was collected by George Gustavson from Paul Kane, a Eskimo who belonged to the Egulac tribe. It was published in 1899 in Gustavson's book Eskimo Songs and Stories.

Other versions
In 1901, a journalist by the name of William Wallace Collier reconstructed Gustavson's story "Two Young Men from Egulac" as an article on the St. Lawrence Episcopy. The story was printed in the June 18, 1901, edition of the Oshweken Times.

Analysis
This legend is told by the Algonquin people of Canada.  It shows how the Algonquin people respected the animals and the rivers and did not hunt unless they had to.  It also shows how they were in tune with the natural world around them and were aware of the dangers that came with hunting.  The legend is a warning about greed and ignoring the natural world.  If the men had not been so desperate to hunt seals and had respected the river, then the water monster would not have been provoked and the man who was swallowed would have been able to stay alive.  The legend also shows that the Algonquin people believed that there was a spirit world and that the water monsters were a part of that world. Analysis

Interpretation
This story is an example of a common theme in Inuit folklore.  Because the Inuit relied on hunting for their food, accidents on the hunt were relatively common.  In this story, the people from Egulac were searching for ducks and mistook two young men lying on the shore for dead.  They assumed that the two men had died searching for food and made a big effort to give them proper burials.  When the men stood up and said that they were not dead, the people were very embarrassed and went to the beach to apologize.

Variations
This story is found in a number of variations.  In one variation, the two young men were searching for polar bears and fell through the ice and into the water.  In another variation, the two young men were out in a canoe and were carried out to sea by the current.  In all of the variations, the people from the village made an effort to give the men proper burials.

Interpretation
The story of "The Singing Tree" is an example of a common Arctic theme found in the folklore of many indigenous cultures.  The theme of a community needing to reaffirm its traditional values and practices in the face of disruptive forces is central to this narrative.  In this story, the singing tree represents the gift of song which unites the community and allows the hunters to continue providing meat for the community.  Without the singers and the songs, the community would starve.  Thus, the story emphasizes the importance of community and the duties and responsibilities of individuals within that community.  It also represents the idea that human actions have consequences and that those consequences can be positive or negative.  In this story, the positive consequence is the reaffirmation of traditional culture and the negative consequence is the disruption of that culture, which could lead to the starvation of the community.

This story comes from the nuu'mas, or secret traditions, of the Natives of Sallish septs (bands) of the coast of British Columbia. It was recorded by John Marr in 1978 from Philip Alethe, a member of the Tsamysalangwa Sallish (Snuneymux). It is a common motif in Native literature and was probably chosen by Marr because of its teaching about the consequences of carelessness and the importance of being fully aware of one's actions.

Analysis
The story is a parable about the dangers of carelessness and the importance of being fully aware of one's actions. The two young men are out hunting, possibly symbolizing the hunt for knowledge or the hunt for women. One is the active seeker of knowledge or women, the other is the more reserved and careful one. The seeker of knowledge or women is also referred to as the "younger one", which can represent innocence or inexperience.
The story takes place "one night two" which can signify that the actions of the two men took place over a period of two nights. The first night the men set out on their hunt and one of them shoots at a seal. In the darkness he mistakes his friend for a seal and shoots him, accidentally killing him. In the morning the two men continue their hunt but the one who was shot is now the hunter and the one who was previously the hunter is now the prey. This shows that sometimes our roles in life can change depending on the situation.

In this story, the two young men are on a hunting trip alone, which is a common element of the hunting story. The cause of death varies in these stories; in "The Boy Who Turned Into a Bear," the young man turns into a bear and is killed by other bears, while in "The Blind Man and the Two Boys," the young man falls into a trap and dies. In "The Boy Who Died of Fright," the cause of death is not explicitly stated, but the title suggests that the young man dies of fear. Like many Arctic stories, this myth includes an element of the supernatural, in which a boy can transform into another animal.This story has been interpreted as an explanation for how people came to live in the Arctic. In Inuit mythology, the world was created from the blood of a slain monster, and all people alive today are the descendants of that monster. Since this story explains how a young man came to die and thus became part of the population, it is a creation story. It also explains why there are no women in Inuit society, as all women are the transformed daughters of the same monster.

This story is told in the Yukon Territory and relates a common theme found in many Indigenous stories, that of "having sex with the wrong being" and the consequences that follow. Story analysis
This story is an example of a trickster tale. In this case, the trick is played on the Egulac men by the people from across the bay. The Egulac men are tricked into giving away all their seals, leaving them with nothing. The story is told to teach a moral lesson about being aware of one's surroundings and being cautious when dealing with others, especially strangers.

This story has variations among the Nuu-chah-nulth. In one version, the Egulac people are not specifically identified as seal hunters. In another variation, the people from across the bay are described as having pale skin and long hair, and are called "the whites."

Background
This story is from the Natives of British Columbia. It is a explanation for why there are so few men from Egulac and why they hardly ever go out on the water.

Analysis
This story is similar to the story of "The Lost Boys" from English folklore. Both of these stories have similar themes of being misunderstood by others and being abandoned. In "The Lost Boys" it is the mother's failure to realize that her boys have grown up and do not need her anymore. In "The Two Young Men from Egulac" it is the people from Egulac failing to realize that the two men are competent enough to go out on the water by themselves and leave them at the river. Both stories have an element of magic, in "The Lost Boys" it is the enchantment of the house that keeps the mother from realizing that her boys have grown up. In "The Two Young Men from Egulac" it is the magic of the fog that covers the river. Both stories have an unhappy ending, in "The Lost Boys" it is the death of the boys. In "The Two Young Men from Egulac" it is the men being left on the river and never heard from again.

Then the people from the other side of the river came over, because they saw the fire that the Egulac people had made to roast the seals. And when the Egulac people saw that they had come, they were glad, and they gave the other side of the river their share of the seals that they had hunted. But the people from the other side of the river said that it was not fair that they should get so much medicine from the river, and they demanded that the Egulac people give them some of the medicine that they had. But the Egulac people said that it was not good medicine that they were giving away, and that they should give the other side of the river some of the birch bark that they had in order to show them that they had been given medicine. And so the Egulac people gave the other side of the river some birch bark, and the people from the other side of the river gave the Egulac people some potato plants for food when the hunting was over. And so the negotiation went on for some time, and when the Egulac people thought that they had gotten enough potato plants they went home.
The Tlingit people tell this story to illustrate how trading with neighbors could be done in a spirit of friendship and generosity, and how important it was to have friends and allies.  It is a story of a time when the spirits of the animals were willing to give themselves up for the benefit of the people, and a time when the gift of potato plants from the other side of the river brought a prosperous harvest.

History
The story is an example of a type of oral literature known as a riddle. Its meaning is evident but its truth is not. Its purpose is to entertain and elicit a response from the audience. This story is told by the Nuu-chah-nulth (or Nukwas) people of the Canadian Pacific Northwest. It is found in the collections of both Frank Speck and George Macdonald. It was also recorded by Marius Campbell in 1968 from Sisha Larson. Among the Nuu-chah-nulth, this story is associated with the transformation of the sea otter.

Analysis
The story consists of a series of statements with no apparent connection, apart from the fact that they all involve actions taking place at the river. The first two statements are questions, stating that two young men went down to the river, but do not specify which two. The third statement is a statement of fact, giving information about the actions of the people from Egulac. The fourth statement is another question, asking which two young men went to the river. The answer is given in the fifth statement, but this statement itself is presented as a question. The sixth statement is a statement of fact, repeating information given in the third statement. The seventh statement is another question, asking which two young men went to the river and brought back seals. The answer is given in the eighth statement, but this statement itself is presented as a question. The ninth statement is a statement of fact, repeating information given in the third and sixth statements. The tenth statement is a question, asking which two young men went to the river and did not bring back seals. The answer is given in the eleventh statement, but this statement itself is presented as a question.

Recording
In 1969, Professor Richard Dauermann of the University of Alaska recorded a story told by a Tlingit elder, Frank Day, who was from Sitka.  The story was recorded on audio tape, and was transcribed by Mary W. Korn, a professor at the University of Alaska.  The transcribed story was then retold by Robert Emory in 1981, trying to remain as close as possible to the original tale as told by Frank Day.  Emory added an introductory paragraph and a concluding paragraph to the story, to provide some cultural context.  The story was then illustrated by the Tlingit artist James Lindsey.  Lindsey's original illustrations were lost, but were later re-created by the artist.  The story was published in 1984 by the University of Alaska Press.  It has also been published in French.

Then the people from the village began to come out and as they came out they were changed into seals. When the two young hunters saw this, they knew that it was time for them to go home, so they changed back into their human form and went back to the village.

History
This story is one of several similar stories found in the collection of oral history recorded by Francis Carl Mallery in the early 1900s. It is one of two stories in the collection that feature hunters who are forced to flee back to their village to avoid being trapped in their transformations.  The egg at the beginning of the story is likely a reference to the creation story of the Tlingit people, who were said to have emerged from an egg. The story itself may be a variant of the more widely known story "The Boy Who Was Turned into a Seal."

Analysis
This story, like many others in the same collection, feature the theme of humans being transformed into animals, and animals being transformed into humans. These transformations often happen as a form of punishment, or as a way to teach a lesson about life. In this story, the two young men are transformed into seals as a way to teach them a lesson about being aware of their surroundings and being mindful of when it is time to go home.

Background
The story comes from the Yupik Eskimos of the Bering Sea. It is an example of a "no survivor" story, a type of folktale common among Eskimos. Such tales are usually explained as caused by the fault of one of the two men involved. In this story, it was the fault of the second man. Another such story is "The Blind Man and the Two Boys".

Analysis
The story is a variation of a more widespread folktale found among many Native American groups.  The story probably derives from a true event.  The lack of a survivor makes this story unique among Native American folktales.  The story seems to be a cautionary tale about going out on the water in a canoe by yourself or with only one other person.

Variants
There is a Siberian variant of this story in which two young men go out on the ocean in a kayak and one falls asleep.  When the sleepy man awakes he finds that his partner has disappeared.  He then paddles around for some time trying to find his partner but fails and begins to think that his partner is no longer alive.  He eventually gives up and returns home.

Background
This story is from the Egulac tribe of the Eskimo people. The land of the Egulac was located somewhere on the southeast coast of Baffin Island, within the modern-day territory of Nunavut, Canada. The date this story was recorded is unknown, but it was probably in the early 1900s. At this time, the people of Egulac were forced to move from their traditional lands due to interactions with outsiders and diseases. They moved north to the area around Pond Inlet, where they established a mission. The story was probably recorded by either a priest or a tribal elder.
The heroes of this story are two young men named Avasura and Kudluk. They are going down to the river to hunt seals, which was a common occupation among Eskimo people.

The story
One night two young men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and passed a large pool where the seals were known to come. The pool was shallow and the bottom was covered with smooth stones. There were no currents or tides in the river, and the water was still and dark as night. The two young men took up positions on either side of the pool, ready to catch the seals that would soon be coming.
Suddenly, a thick fog came down, covering the water, the shore, and the surrounding land. The fog was so thick that one could not see a hand held at arm's length. The stillness was broken only by the sounds of the river, and the cries of the birds that occasionally broke the silence.
As they stood there, the two young men heard voices behind them. They turned around and saw a group of people coming towards them. They were surprised and frightened by this, for they had been alone, and now here was this group of people coming towards them.
The people

Then all of a sudden, a big monster appeared and began to pursue the two men. One of them managed to jump into the water and swim to the shore, but the other one was caught by the monster and was dragged under the water.
As the men were from Egulac, they had each other's backs, and the one who had been left behind took up a weapon and went back to fight the monster. He caught it by its tail and dragged it to the shore, where he crushed its head with a stone.
After that, the two men went back to their village, where they were welcomed as heroes.
When the chief of the village heard the story, he decided that it was time to go to war with the villagers from the nearby village, for he was convinced that it was their fault that the monster appeared.
So, the villagers from Egulac gathered weapons and went to the village next door, ready to fight.
But just as they were about to start the battle, the other village sent a delegation with apologies, gifts and peace offerings.
The chief of Egulac accepted the offer and made peace with the neighboring village.
From that day on, the two villages were in peace, even more strongly bonded by their common enemy.

The story is a variant of the common international Cinderella story, with elements of "The Fable of the Two Foxes" and "The Magic Brush" also present.  The two young men are like Cinderella's sisters, and the seven creatures that cause the fog are like the fairy godmother.  The woman who keeps the young man from crossing the river is Cinderella herself, and the last man is Cinderella's unknown husband (or her future husband, if we consider the time between the telling of the story and its eventual ending).  The river is the boundary between the familiar world and the unknown world, and crossing the river is like entering adulthood.  The story warns young people not to be in a hurry to become adults, and not to be swayed by offers of power or riches, as the consequences of such actions can be severe.

It is a classic example of a traditional Nuu-chah-nulth oral story. It contains many of the typical elements of such stories:  a journey, an encounter with a supernatural being, a test of wits and courage, and a return to the community.  This particular story also reflects an important aspect of Nuu-chah-nulth culture, the respect for and dependence on the natural world, and the dangers of ignoring that world's rules.

Analyzing the situation
The men knew they had to do something to get off the island, so they decided to build a fire and wait for morning so they could see which direction to go in. As they were gathering wood for the fire, one of the men found a berry bush and ate some berries. Suddenly, he felt dizzy and fell asleep. When he woke up, the other man was gone. He looked around and saw footprints in the sand, leading to the shore. He followed them and found the other man standing at the water's edge, ready to swim back to the shore. The first man realized that the footprints he had been following were not his own, and that he had been heading in the wrong direction. He turned around and followed the footprints he had been leaving in the sand back to the place where he had found the berry bush. He knew that those footprints would take him back to the place where he had come from, and he followed them until he got back to the shore.

Living on Egulac

They laid a trap for seals, and when they had enough meat, they went to yet another place on the island and built another fire. Analytical essay
This is a classic example of a colonial encounter, in which the technological superiority of the Egulacs allows them to easily subjugate the less technologically advanced Kanaulas.  The Egulacs' ability to hunt seal is what ultimately saves the Kanaulas from being slaughtered, demonstrating both the utility and the danger of bringing guns to a spear fight.
While the Egulacs are portrayed as the aggressors in this tale, they are also shown to be capable of compassion.  By bringing the seal back to the village, they effectively saved the Kanaulas from certain death, thereby demonstrating both the benevolence and the ruthlessness of colonial powers.

So the two young men swam over to the other side of the river and helped the people get their nets and food supplies back to their homes on the shore.  After the two young men helped the people, they gave thanks and paid the two men for their help with their highest quality food and hunting equipment.  However, when the two young men got back to their side of the river, they saw that their village had been raided and their women and children had been kidnapped by the Bugus.  The two young men then vowed to go after the raiders and get their village back.  The story is told in "The Adventures of Two Young Men" a traditional story told by the Alutiiq people of the Native Village of Port Graham on the Kenai Peninsula in South Central Alaska.

Retelling
Once upon a time, there was a king who lived by the sea.  He was a powerful man, but he was kind to his people.  He had two sons, who were strong swimmers.  They spent most of their time hunting seal along the coast.
One night, the two sons went out to hunt seals, but they took their mother's best paddle with them.  It was a beautiful paddle, carved from a single piece of wood.  The two sons went to the other side of the river, where there was a large seal rookery.  They paddled up to the shore and saw a seal, but before they could shoot it, a large fog rolled in.  The two men waited for the fog to clear, but it did not.  They decided to swim for the other side of the river, where they knew there was a village.  They swam and swam, until they were almost too tired to swim.  Then they saw the village, and they were amazed at how close they had come to the enemy's land.

Then the people from the village came out to hunt for seals by the light of the moon, but they could not find any because the seals were all hiding in the fog.  The villagers yelled at the two young men, saying, "You have ruined our livelihood!  From now on you will have to support us.  You are the cause of our fate."  The two young men were frightened and went back to the village.  They did not return to hunting for seal for a whole year.  During that time the village became very poor and there was not enough food.  The people were forced to leave their homes and move to the coast.  When the men from Egulac went out to hunt seals again, they were very careful not to disrupt the lives of the seals.  They dug holes in the sand and put fish in them to lure the seals out of the water.  This worked and soon the men from Egulac had more than they could eat.  They decided to share their bounty with the other villages and this made the people very happy.  From that time on the men from Egulac were respected by all the neighboring villages.

This story is told by the people of Saksak, a village located on the southeastern coast of Unalaska Island.  It demonstrates the important role respect plays in the lives of the Saksak people.  Without respecting the balance of nature and the needs of other villages, the people from Egulac would have suffered the consequences of their actions.  By sharing their bounty with others, the people earned respect and friendship.

The monster could also breathe underwater, which made it hard for the Algonquin people to avoid it. Sometimes the monster would transform into the shape of a beautiful woman to lure men to it. But, in the end, it would drown them or kill them in some other way.

The story of the two young men and the water monsters is told in many different versions. Sometimes the monsters are described as Gugul, or as a giant octopus with arms that can reach more than a man's height. Sometimes the monsters are said to live in the bay, and sometimes they are said to live far out in the sea. Sometimes the monsters attack seals, and sometimes they attack men. But, in all the versions, the monsters are there to scare men so that they will not go out on the water.

Analysis
This legend shows how the people of Egulac viewed the world and their position in it.  They saw the world as a dangerous place, filled with supernatural forces that could harm them at any time.  The fog was personified as a being that could hide the hunters from their prey, and the screams in the night were probably made by some sort of animal, possibly a seal, but in the minds of the Egulac it could have been anything from a giant octopus to a band of thieving ghosts.  The raid by the Beleaguered People illustrated the vulnerability of the Egulac to attack from their neighbors, and the need to always be on guard against the possibility of ambush.

Sources
This legend was recorded by Franz Boas in 1890, in an article titled "Materials for a Comparative Study of the Culture of the Eskimo," in the Fourth Annual Report of the Bureau of American Ethnology. It was reprinted in 1961, along with a number of other articles on Arctic cultures, in a book titled Eskimo: Race, Culture, and Modernization.  It can also be found in a 1936 article in The Journal of American Folklore, in an article on Alaskan Eskimo materials collected by George W. Vincent.

The village mourned for them, and the people went about their tasks in a sad state of mind.  Finally, after a long time, one of the young men was found, floating in the river.  He was dead, but the other one was never found.  The village was very sad, and no one knew why the one young man was spared while the other was not.  They did not know if it was related to the fact that he was a better swimmer, or if it was just luck that he was found.  The mystery was never solved, and the people eventually forgot about it, though they would sometimes see the young man in their dreams.  During the night, whenever the fog rolls in, the people of Egulac hear the crying of the young man, and some say it is the lost boy, still lost in the river.

This story was told by the people of Nunavut, Canada, to illustrate the concept of "it happens like this" or "this is how it is".  It shows how harsh and unfair life can be, and how sometimes things just "happen".  The story also shows how important community support is, as the people of the village mourned together and supported one another through the loss of the young men.

History
This story was recorded by George Macdonald in 1902, from a young man named Ephriam Kalmakoff who said it was a story told by elders of his tribe. It was thought that this story may have originated in the southern part of the Seward Peninsula, Alaska.

Analysis
This story is an example of a kind of folklore known as "revenge tales", in which a group of people suffer some form of interference or harm from a non-human group, and plan and carry out a violent attack in retaliation. In this story, the humans suffer no direct harm from the seal-people, but one may infer that they assume the seal-people are responsible for the disappearance of the two hunters, and take violent revenge without trying to determine if there was some other cause for the disappearance. The story also exhibits elements of a more general class of folktales known as "transformation tales", in which human beings are transformed into animals or into some other form of being.

Background
This story comes from the Tlingit people of the Northwest Coast of North America. It was recorded by Dr. George W. Elcock in 1963 from Frank Williams, a teacher and assistant tribal councilman of the Tlingit.

Analysis
This story shows the importance of revenge in Tlingit culture.  When the men from Egulac were killed by the men from the village, the men from Egulac sought to avenge their comrades by killing all the men from the village, except for the two who were hiding.  This desire for revenge drove the men from Egulac to ignore the fact that the men from the village had been killing them for their own food supply.  Instead, the men from Egulac focused on avenging their comrades, even though many of them knew that this would mean their own deaths.  The story shows that, in Tlingit culture, the desire for revenge was so strong that it overrode any consideration of self-preservation.

The story tells how the people from Egulac were better hunters and therefore more valuable than the people from the other side of the river.

Analysis
The story probably arose out of actual events.  The Egulac people probably did often hunt seals and share the prey with the people from the other side of the river, but in larger numbers and/or more regularly than the people from the other side of the river.  Over time the people from Egulac came to believe that they were the only true hunters and that the people from the other side of the river were merely auxiliary.  The story probably served to justify the social and hunting limitations imposed on the people from the other side of the river by the people from Egulac.

Background
This story is from the people from the Kwanlin Dén Alaska Native Tribe located near Bethel, Alaska. Analysis

Then the people from each of the four neighboring tribes came down to the river one by one, silently, so as not to disturb the Egulac people. When the Egulac people were asleep, the other tribes took their canoes and silently pulled them to the Egulac camp. When the morning dawned and the fog lifted, the Egulac people were surprised and angry to see canoes from the other tribes at their camp.

Background
The story is a example of a type of oral literature known as a "giveaway story". In such stories, a group of people share a resource (in this case, the location of a seal rookery) and one group quietly takes more than its fair share, causing resentment and possible retaliation from the aggrieved parties. Such stories warn children (and adults) not to be greedy, not to take more than is fair, and not to be arrogant towards members of one's community.

Analysis
This story is told by the Nuučánał (Nukatel) people, who are part of the Eskimo-Naumi people of the Northwest Coast of North America. The story is found in the collections of the Canadian Museum of History and the University of Alaska, and was recorded in 1970 by Andrew D. Maschado, a teacher and ethnographer. Although the story is of a specific cultural origin, its themes of sharing, greed, and retaliation are universal.

Variants
There are many variations of this story.  In one version, the Egulac people are the only ones who can see the seal rookery, and all the other tribes are jealous of them. In another variation, the Egulac people are the only ones who can catch the seals, and all the other tribes are envious of them. In yet another variation, the other tribes are stealing the Egulac people's seals.

Background
This is a story from the P.E.I. section of the Confederacy of the Dene, retold by Elder William Commons. It shows how the people were organized into small groups that would go out hunting, and how they depended on each other for protection from both outside dangers and dangers within the community.

Main events
Two young men go out to the river to hunt seals.
It becomes foggy and calm.
The people from the village shout, scream, and beat their drums and guns because they are afraid the hunters will come back.
The young men stay until morning and go back to the village.
From then on the people do not go out into the river to hunt seals.

Moral
The moral of the story is that the people should not be afraid of the unknown and should trust each other.

Analysis
This story shows how the people were organized into small hunting groups that went out and came back at specific times. It also shows how important communication was within the community. If the hunters had come back, there would have been a lack of food and the community would have suffered. Therefore, the people had to coordinate their hunting trips in order to ensure there was enough food for everyone. The community's reaction shows how easy it was for people to panic and how a lack of communication could have disastrous consequences.

They went toward it and found it was coming from a small cave in the bank of the river. As they entered the cave they saw a beautiful young woman sitting on a stone throwing a spear at a seal. Analysis
This story is an example of a genre of folklore known as "courtship stories", in which a man (or woman) encounters a supernatural being (usually a god, goddess, or fey) who offers to grant wishes or bestow blessings if the person will only spend time with them. In this story, the two young men from Egulac are out hunting one night when they come across a beautiful woman who invites them to spend the night with her. Each of the men makes a wish, and their wishes come true, but at a later time the woman disappears, leaving the men to wonder if their dreams have come true. The story suggests that the woman the men encountered was most likely a mermaid, given that she is described as beautiful, other-worldly, and associated with the sea.

Importance
This story is important in Kwakwaka'wakw culture because it shows the negative consequences of greed and fighting. It also shows the importance of respecting the land and nature.

There are a few different variants of this story. In one variation, the two men are not from Egulac, but rather are visitors who came to the river to hunt seals. In this version, the woman is described as a sea-goddess. In another variation, the two men are from neighboring clans and are not from Egulac. In still another variation, the two men are brothers. In all of these variations, the story follows the same basic plot.

The tale of the Two Young Men and the Sea-Monsters is an example of a common motif in Native Canadian literature, namely, the fear of the supernatural.  In this story, the supernatural is represented by the evil spirits that inhabit the bottom of the river.  These spirits are capable of terrifying native fisherman into fleeing for their lives, thereby preventing the fisherman from practising their trade.
As in many other Native Canadian stories, the theme of the dangers of the supernatural is combined with an account of a specific place.  In this story, the specific place is the "river" which is apparently located near Egulac (or Egasant), a Native Canadian settlement on the west coast of Vancouver Island.  The combination of place and theme is typical of Native Canadian literature, as it allows the listener/reader to easily visualize the story.  The story also provides an explanation as to why the natives avoided a certain area, thus preserving the unity of the community by avoiding conflict with the supernatural.
The tale of the Two Young Men and the Sea-Monsters is a fairly long story, containing many repetitions.  These repetitions serve to emphasize the frightfulness of the supernatural, as well as the foolishness of the two young men who ignored the warnings of their elders and went down to the river anyway. Background
This story comes from the Nuuchiq'yuut Lox, or Eskimo National Anthem. It describes an incident that occurred in Adamlik, a former whaling village on the southeast edge of Victoria Island, in the Yukon territory of Canada. The date of the incident is not known, but it likely occurred in the late 1800s or early 1900s. The two young men from Egulac are thought to be Vukodar and Puvukak, who were either brothers or very close friends.

Analysis
This story illustrates a number of important aspects of Nuuchiq (Eskimo) culture. First, it describes the important role that hunting and the harvesting of seals in particular plays in the lives of Nuuchiq people. Second, it describes the communal nature of Nuuchiq society, in which the needs and welfare of the group as a whole takes priority over the needs of the individual. This is why the people from the village shouted to the two young hunters to leave the beach, even though doing so would mean that the young men would be unable to participate in the upcoming battle and thus fail to contribute to the welfare of the group. Lastly, this story describes the high value that Nuuchiq people place on courage and physical strength, as the young men are described as being very strong and fierce fighters.

The fog made the river invisible, so the two men got lost and were unable to find their way back to their village. They kept walking along the shore until they came upon a strange village with fancy houses made from blocks of stone. A woman came out of one of the houses and invited the two men into her home. She gave them food and tried to convince them to stay with her people. The two men refused and continued on their journey. As they got farther away from the village, the fog cleared, and the sun rose. Then the men realized that they had been led away from their own village by the evil woman from the strange village. They quickly rushed back to their own village, where they arrived just as the morning star was rising.

Analysis
This story includes many common elements of traditional Inuit tales. It involves a journey with a supernatural element, a mistake or decision that must be rectified, and a warning about the consequences of staying with outsiders. The story also contains an element of sexuality, with the woman from the other village attempting to keep the men with her. This story, however, is a unique version of the common Inuit tale of the fog that causes people to get lost. In most versions, it is the cold and darkness that are the dangers, and getting lost is a more direct consequence of wandering in the fog. In this tale, the listener is left to assume that the evil woman led the men astray intentionally, perhaps to sacrifice them to whatever evil spirits she served. The tale thus contains an element of fear of women, a common theme in many Inuit stories.

This story can be interpreted on several levels. This legend comes from the people of Egulac (or Eglac), who lived along the west coast of Hudson Bay at a place called Fort George. The date this tale was recorded is unknown, but it was likely recorded in the late 19th century.

Analysis
This tale is an example of a seal-hero story, a type of story that was told by many Native American groups. In these stories, a hero sets out on a journey and encounters many challenges, usually involving animals. In this story, the hero is a "young man," probably meaning a teenage boy. The boy goes out to hunt seals, a common activity along the coast of the Arctic Ocean. While he is out, a kidnapping occurs in his village. Upon returning home, the boy is accused of the kidnapping, but he denies it and explains that someone else must be responsible. The villagers decide to go out and look for the kidnapper, leaving the boy at home. When the villagers return, they realize that the boy was telling the truth and that it was the white man who had seized their leader. In the end, the hero goes back out to hunt seals, proving his innocence.

Importance
This story is important in the culture of the people of Saddle Lake Cree Nation, located in northwestern Alberta, Canada. It demonstrates the dangers of going onto the water without proper preparation and without respecting the laws of the river. It also shows the negative consequences of greed and impatience.

Source
The story was recorded in 1970 by a Saddle Lake elder named Edward Osborne.

Variations
There is a slightly different version of this story recorded in Janice Acoose's book, Elders' Teachings: Stories and Tips for Living. In this version, the two young men are named Pete and Billy. They go down to the river to get drunk and forget that they are hunting. When they have had enough to drink, Billy suggests that they go out on the water in the canoe to see which one of them can catch the most seals. As they are rowing out to the middle of the lake, Pete says that he is tired and wants to turn back, but Billy talks him into staying. Suddenly, the water monsters appear and the canoe capsizes, throwing the two young men into the water where they drown.

Analysis
This story can be analyzed using the hero's journey. In this story, the two young men are the heroes. They set out on a journey to the river, but they are not prepared and are soon faced with danger in the form of the water monsters. Despite the warnings and the pleas of Pete to turn back, Billy convinces him to keep going and he ends up getting the two of them killed.

Analysis
In this story, the two hunters are able to convince the village that they were not witches through logical reasoning and by providing evidence.  However, it was the chief's authority that ultimately halted the villagers from burning the hunters at the stake.  This shows the hierarchical organization of the village and the importance of the chief as a decision maker.  The story also highlights the negative consequences of panic and fear, as the villagers were prepared to burn two innocent men at the stake without sufficient evidence.

The story also shows how the harvest was more important than the hunt. In this story, the hunt was disrupted by the fog, which allowed the hunters to hunt in the first place, but prevented the villagers from catching the seals themselves.  Thus, the hunters were able to gather a large amount of food before the harvests began, ensuring that there would be plenty of food for the winter.

Background
This story is a part of the traditional lore of the Nuuchiq people and was recorded by Roald Nellemann in 1916. It was also recorded by F. Vasiliev in 1904. According to Nellemann, this story was told by an old Tundra Eskimo who was living in Bethel at the time.

Analysis
This story is an example of a Strokes Tale, a genre of Eskimo oral literature in which a heroic figure uses a tool made of bone or ivory to overcome an adversary. In this story, the two young men are the strokes tale heroes. They are described as being nimble and skillful hunters who were able to keep up with the swift seals they were chasing. Despite their fine motor skills, they were unable to avoid being killed by the tide. Their bodies were washed out to sea and were never recovered, making this story a sad tale of lost youth.

Suddenly, the people from the village came out of their houses and began to shout and scream, saying things like, "Kill them! They are killing us!" Description of the painting
In the painting, we see six people from Egulac (three on either side of the canoe) pulling towards the viewer while a seventh person (on the right) is pushing a carcass towards the canoe. There is a pale green sea monster lying on the bottom of the lake and a school of fish swimming by. There are also two harp seals floating on their backs.One of the men has a large reddish-brown scar across his chest and another has a small blue scar on his forehead. Both of these scars are references to real-life scars that Serrell had on his body. The six men in the canoe are also a reference to Serrell's six sons. The painted tin can and rifle barrels on the bottom of the lake are references to Serrell's waste materials from his printing processes. The wave patterns on the lake are also a reference to Serrell's prints.

Interpretation
This painting is one of a series of works that Serrell created after a trip he took up the east coast of Canada. During this trip, Serrell visited a number of Inuit communities and established relationships with a number of Inuit families. The images in this series were derived from stories told to Serrell by members of these communities. For Serrell, these stories provided a connection to the land and a sense of belonging that he had been searching for throughout his life.
Although Serrell had a deep respect for the Inuit people and their culture, he did not consider himself to be an Inuit artist. He felt that it was not his place to appropriate the forms and motifs of Inuit art. However, he did feel that he was entitled to use the stories that were told to him as a white man who had established a relationship with an Inuit family.

Analysis
This story suggests that while hunting is an important activity in Inuit culture, it is not the only thing that is valuable.  The two men were willing to risk their lives to get food, but they also knew when it was time to stop and rest.  Even though they were tired and hungry, they did not keep hunting but instead focused on getting sleep.  This shows a balance between the importance of physical needs and the need to rest.
