Background
The tale begins with two young hunters named Hylak and Owlalus, who lived near a large egulac (a species of seal) rookery on an island off the coast of what is now Vancouver Island. The two friends often went down to the river to hunt seals and have fun.
One night, as they were sitting by the fire, Hylak said he was going to fetch firewood and left Owlalus sitting by the fire. But when Hylak returned, Owlalus had vanished. Hylak searched for his friend but could not find him, and eventually returned to the rookery without him.
Later, the tribe's medicine man explained to Hylak that while he was gone, the spirits of the egulac had appeared to the two hunters, forming a wall in front of them. Although Hylak had stood bravely facing the spirits, his friend Owlalus had been afraid and tried to run away. In the end, Owlalus had been carried off by the spirits, and Hylak was left to return to the village alone.

Variants
This tale is mostly found among the tribes of the Kwakiutl. A variant of this story is told among the Bella Coola, in which the two hunters are named Yeh-hee-yu and Wadu-wadu. In this version, the wall of spirits was formed by the winds of the different tribes, and the spirits of the human hunters were transformed into the winds of the tribes.

Analysis
This is an example of an indirect object: the bullet.  The sentence is structured in a way that makes the reader realize what really happened only at the end.  The use of the passive voice ("the bullet struck him") makes the reader feel as if they are not directly responsible for the action of the sentence.  The consequence of the action is also hidden from the reader until the end, making the story more engaging and causing the reader to feel a stronger emotional response when they realize what has happened.

Eventually, only the skeletal remains of the two men were found on the shore of the island.

Interpretation
Moose hide containers were found near the site, containing red ochre and smoking pipes.  The smoking pipes were made from the tubes of other pipes, and were likely used by the men before and after they entered the canoe.  The scene depicted on the pipes was probably meant to be a literal representation of an incident that occurred between two men from the Egulac group, and was engraved on the pipes as a form of history or warning.  The two men may have been from different clans, as war paint was found on the faces of the figures.  It is also possible that the two men represented the qualities of a stereotypical hero and villain, as one man seems to be depicted as a tyyuu (demon) and the other as a hero.  The hero is shown with a large nose and a small mouth, indicating that he may have been a good leader and communicator.  The tyyuu (demon) is shown with a large mouth and no nose, indicating that he may have been a greedy and unfair leader.  These negative qualities are further emphasized by the fact that they were left behind by their people to die, indicating that they were probably expelled from the village for their selfish and greedy behaviors.

Analysis
This story demonstrates the negative effects of industrialization on the lives of Native Americans. In this story, the people from the village are prevented from easily accessing the resources they need to survive, and are forced to find new ways of making a living. The story also shows how easily communication can be hindered by differences in language and by the inability of those who are communicating to see each other clearly.

This is a tale from the Algonquian language group, told by the Sainte Croix Tribe of the Wisconsin River. It was recorded by Frank Speck in 1928.

Analysis
This tale is an example of a transformational tale, or a tale that involves a transformation.  It also involves a conflict, which is a common element in transformational tales.  In this tale, the conflict is between the people from across the river and the two young men from Egulac.  When the people from across the river first arrived, the two young men from Egulac did not understand them, and so they fought.  This fighting possibly stemmed from the fact that the people from Egulac were different from the people across the river, and so they did not communicate in the same way.  The fighting also may have been caused by tension and hostility between the two groups.  These tensions may have been heightened by the fact that the two groups were in competition with one another, as they were likely to be in a mutual hunting area.  The fighting probably continued until the sun came up because the people from Egulac were exhausted from fighting

Then the people from the village came out and began to shout and scream and the two young men were frightened and forgot to breathe properly and both of them dropped down dead.

Background
This story is told by Tlingit storyteller Peter J. Goldfinch (1998). It is a member of the "Raven cycle" of stories, and is told to explain why there are no seals along the inside Passage of the Aleutian Islands. According to Goldfinch, the story was told to him by  a man named Axtup.

Analysis
Anthropologist William Reid points out that despite the similarity in name, the Raven cycle of stories has very little in common with the stories told in the Eskimo cycle of stories. In this story, Reid sees an example of a type of story found in many Northwest Coast cultures, the "Failure to Communicate" story. In these stories, two or more characters fail to communicate properly, and as a result, one or more of them die. In this story, the two hunters fail to realize that they need to breathe while they are out on the boat, and as a result, they die. Reid also points out that the story has elements of both trickster and hero stories. The two hunters are tricked by the birds (seagulls), but in the end, it is their own actions that result in their death.

The story
This story goes back a long time ago when people from the village went down to the river to hunt seals. It was a nice day, the sun was shining, there was a light breeze, and the two young men from Egulac were excited to go seal hunting. They set out in their canoe, paddled out to the middle of the river, and began singing a seal call. Suddenly, a seal appeared, but as the two men were about to shoot it, a shaman appeared out of nowhere and said, "No, don't shoot that seal. It is not the right time." The young men paid no attention to the shaman and shot the seal. As they were carrying the seal back to the canoe, a big wave came and washed the young men into the river. The canoe was carried away and the two men were lost.
The people from the village were afraid to go out in the canoes any more, especially by themselves. They decided that they would always take a shaman with them to protect them.

Recognition
In 1954, when the men of Egulac were asked to identify a sketch of the creature made by artist John Brown, they immediately recognised it as the same creature they had seen in 1940. The artist had captured the creature's distinct head shape, small dorsal fin, and long tail. The men of Egulac had named the creature "Le Viperge" (French for "The Serpentine One"), and believed that it was a large eel. They avoided the river for many years after the initial sighting, until a group of boys convinced them to return in 1955. When the creature was first sighted in 1940, it was thought by the locals to be a war-wounded German submarine, and was given the name "The Beast of Loch Ness". The beast was first brought to international attention on 14 April 1950, when a London newspaper ran a story about the creature with the headline "Scottish Loch Ness 'Monster'".The popular perception of the Loch Ness Monster as a water-dwelling cryptid was established in 1960, when a group of scientists investigated the creature's habitat and concluded that there was no evidence to suggest that it was a marine animal. The two young hunters were frightened and they ran away from the river. From that time the people of Egulac laughed at these two young men.

Interpretation
This tale has several versions. In one version, the two young hunters are ridiculed by the other villagers because they were afraid of a human-like creature in the fog, which turned out to be a shaman who was gathering spirits. In another version, the two young men were laughed at for running away from a seal that was only a cub.
The tale is an example of an arrowhead story, a type of story that was told by many Native American groups to explain the origin of a clan or a social custom. In this tale, the two young men represent the ancestors of the Egulac people, and their fear and ridicule is a reminder of the dangers of cowardice and of wasting opportunities.

One man fired a shot at a seal and missed. The bullet went off in the direction of the other man and hit him in the side. The man who was shot died instantly. The man who fired the shot was never seen again. Now, every year during the time of the full moon, the egg hunters from Egulac gather and  conduct a ceremony for the man who died while hunting. They offer seal skins and gifts to the spirit of the man, asking for his help in their hunt.

Interpretation
This story illustrates two important elements of the Alaskan Native culture.  The first is the integration of the supernatural into everyday life.  The men who hunted seals were not simply hunting for food; they were also hunting in order to please the ghost of the man who died while hunting.  The hunt itself was a social event, a time for the men of the tribe to get together and reinforce their social bonds.  The story shows how important it was for the men to maintain good relations with the spirits of the land and the dead, through gifts and ceremonies.
The second important element of the Alaskan Native culture illustrated by this story is the concept of reciprocity.  The men who hunted seals expected to receive seal meat and other supplies in return for their gift to the dead man's spirit.  This reciprocity reinforced the social bonds within the tribe.

Analysis
The story of "The Two Young Men from Egulac" is an example of an arbitrary punishment narrative.  In such stories, someone does something that is considered wrong or unfriendly, and as a result they are punished in some arbitrary way.  In this story, the two young men are punished for refusing to share their meat with the villagers.  The villagers respond by calling the young men names and then physically attacking them, resulting in the death of one of the young men.  The second young man swims away to another village.  The villagers rejoice at the death of the bearded man, saying that there will be no more Egulac men in their village.  The story does not explain why the villagers were drinking from the river in the first place, or why the two young men were hunting seals.  It is also not explained why the second young man did not share the meat of the seal that he caught.  The story does not have a clear moral and leaves the reader to decide for themselves what the moral of the story is.  One possible moral is that it is not wise to anger the people of a certain race or group, as you may suffer the consequences of their anger.

Analysis
This story is one of a number of similar stories found in the southern Pauwues-Porome section of the Bungudore legend cycle.  It shares certain elements with other stories in this cycle, such as the egality of the protagonists and the sense in which the land is seen as being initially uninhabited.  The humour in this story comes largely from the situation in which the Egulac find themselves, being laughed at by the inhabitants of the other side of the harbour for their nakedness.  The story explains the name of a social group, and like many such stories it uses an animal (seal in this case) as the object of the hunt which provides the pretext for the journey and the encounter with the unexpected.  The rise of the tide is used as a narrative device to cover the Egulac's embarrassment and their subsequent abandonment of the hunt.

Background
This story comes from the Nuuchi7inii (Nootka) people of western Vancouver Island. It was recorded in 1920 by George M. Foster, a missionary with the Presbyterian Church.

This story is a good example of a nuuchi7inii ribbon story. It has a clear beginning, middle, and end, and has a moral. In this story, the moral is that "We must always be on the lookout for danger, and be prepared to defend ourselves."

Analysis
This story is told in a number of versions, some of which omit certain details. It is often told along with the story of "Why the Sea is Salted," which immediately follows it in some versions. In common with other stories in this cycle, it explains a natural phenomenon (in this case, the disappearance of two men who were lost in the fog, and the subsequent flooding of the land when the sea rose to cover the trees). 
The story also shares motivational aspects with other Senupic legends.  In common with many other Senupic tales, it teaches respect for elders and warns against alcoholic drink. It also shares an Apollonian/Dionysian motif with other stories, such as "Why the Sea is Salted."

Interpretation
This story is a classic example of a hero journey. The hero is a young man who is chosen by a supernatural being to be a leader or "hero" of some kind. In this story, the Spirit of the River gives the young man gifts and protection, making him a successful hunter and provider for the tribe.

Mythological origins
This story is a Native American one, and was recorded by Francis Healey in 1909 while he was living among the Hupa people. The story itself is believed to be a creation of the Hupa people and is found only among the Hupa and nearby groups.

Comparative analysis
Similar ideas are found in many native cultures.  For example, in the Algonquin culture, the mistletoe is considered to be a "love plant" that produces "love berries."  These ideas are found in the stories of Dashing Deer and The Gift of the West Wind.

Interpretation
This story shows that even though the people from Egulac lost their friends to a seemingly unfortunate event, they were still able to gain something of value in return. And then the people from the other side of the river began to shoot at them and nearly shot them down.  The two Egulac men then swam over to the other side of the river and hid in the long tall grass by the shore.  After that, the men from Egulac began to come over in canoes and take away the children.  The two men from the other side of the river were about to give up and leave, but then they noticed that the Egulac men were taking the children away in canoes and heading up the river.  So the two men from the other side of the river went back and got ready to attack.  But then the Egulac men came back with the children and put them down on the shore.  The two men from the other side of the river were amazed and happy to see the children again.  From then on, the two sides of the river began to trade with each other and the war was forgotten.

Analysis
The story is a relic of an earlier time when the people of the Northwest Coast of North America lived in small, separate tribes and warred with one another.  It shows how important children were to the tribes and how desperately the tribes wanted children.  It also shows how easily wars could break out between the tribes.  Overall, the story shows the harsh conditions of life on the Northwest Coast and how important it was for the tribes to get along with one another.

Mythic meaning
In this story, the two young men from Egulac represent all of the people from that group.  The children represent the future of the groups, and the war between the groups threatens to destroy the future of both groups.  By forgetting the war and making peace, the groups are able to ensure the continuance of the future generations.  The story thus emphasizes the importance of peace and cooperation with neighboring groups for the success and survival of a community.

Then the people from the village began to come out and curse the young men, saying, "You are murderers! You are murderers!"  The two young men were confused and asked each other, "What have we done?"  Then a old man came up to them and said, "You killed the seal pup."  The young men did not understand how the seal pup's death was murder.  The old man then explained that the seal pup was the embodiment of a person's spirit, and when a person's spirit is evil, it takes the form of a seal pup.  The only way to kill an evil spirit is to shoot it with a bullet or a arrow dipped in seal fat.  The young men had not killed the seal pup in self-defense or for the purpose of feeding themselves or their families, so according to the people from the village, they had murdered the seal pup.  The two young men were then forced to carry the seal pup carcass back to the village and bury it.  From then on, the two young men were considered murderers by the people from the village and were avoided.

Analysis
This story is an example of how the Inuit people view the natural world.  According to many Inuit, the world is alive, and everything in it has a soul.  The souls of humans take the form of seals upon death, and thus, killing a sealed is killing a soul.  Thus, murder is a very serious offense in Inuit culture.

Then the people from the village came out and began shouting, "Kill the whites!" Then the two young men were killed and thrown into the water; and for many days the people searched for their bodies, but they could not find them.

Interpretation
This story illustrates an important element of Inuit culture: the importance of the hunt and the land. In this story, the two hunters are killed because they were thought to be taking more than their fair share of the animals. In Inuit culture, the earth and the animals are thought of as living things that must be respected. If the hunters take more than they need, they are thought to be disrespecting the earth and the animals, and therefore the land will give back less. In this story, the land would not give back the bodies of the two hunters, because they were not respected.

Another important element of Inuit culture is illustrated in this story as well.  Inuit often went out on hunting trips alone or in small groups, and would often be gone for days or even weeks at a time.  Because of this, many Inuit hunters carried a sacred object such as a bone or stone to protect them on their trips and to bring back offerings to the land.  In this story, one of the young men had a bone necklace that he wore around his neck, which may have been what the people from the village saw as a "white man's" object, and therefore something to be gotten rid of.

The story is a good example of a folktale, featuring simple language, a small number of characters, and a clear moral. The tale has some similarities to the story of "The Day of the Dead", also told by the Sesame Workshop in 1974. The moral of "The Day of the Dead" is give, while the moral of Kauai is stop killing. Both tales teach the same moral, but in opposite manners. Whereas in "The Day of the Dead", the givers of gifts are the spirits of the dead, in Kauai, the givers of gifts are the children, and the spirits of the dead are the warriors. The tales also feature feasting, but in different contexts; in Kauai, the feasting is part of a peace negotiation, while in The Day of the Dead, the feasting is part of a celebration of life.

His companion agreed, and when he counted to ten, his friend jumped into the water. But when he counted to twenty, his friend was not back in the canoe. He continued to count and when he reached one hundred, he called out in desperation, "My friend, you have lost your way. Come back now." His words echoed through the stillness of the night and the fog. His companion was lost. His words were lost. His friend was lost. And he was alone.

Analysis
This story describes a situation in which two young men are hunting seals and one jumps into the water and swims away. The story uses imagery to describe the hunting scene and the natural surroundings, and also to convey the feeling of loneliness and despair that the narrator feels when his friend does not return. The story emphasizes the importance of communication and the dangers of assuming that others will always be there.

Themes
Loneliness
The story describes a very lonely scene, not only for the narrator, but also for the reader. The narrator is alone in his canoe, hunting in the middle of the night, with nothing but the sound of his own voice to keep him company. His loneliness is increased when his friend jumps into the water and does not return. The narrator’s despair is evident in his pleas for his friend to return: “My friend, you have lost your way. Come back now.” The story highlights the feeling of isolation that can come from assuming that others will always be there and from failing to communicate clearly.

The Story
Once upon a time there was a couple of young men from the village of Egulac, and they were always out looking for adventure.  One night they decided to go down to the river to hunt seals.  They set out in a canoe and paddled out into the middle of the river and waited.  Soon they heard a sound, and when they looked up they saw a pair of glowing eyes, and when they came closer they saw that it was a sea monster.  The monster was so large that its eyes were the only part of it that could be seen above the water.  The two young men were scared out of their wits, and they paddled back to the village as fast as they could.  When they got there they told everyone they had seen a sea monster, but no one believed them.  So the two young men went out every night for a week, and every night they saw the sea monster, and every night the village people didn't believe them.  Finally the young men went to the wise man of the village and told him all that had happened, and the wise man went to the river to see the sea monster for himself.  When the wise man saw the sea monster he was scared, and he ran back to the village and told everyone that it was true, that there was a sea monster in the river.  From that time on the people of Egulac respected the young men, and they went out hunting and fishing with them, and they all made a lot of money.  Eventually the two young men grew old and died, and the stories of the sea monster died with them, but the people of Egulac still spoke of it.

Their flesh was like flesh of mice,
Their fur was like the fur of foxes,
Their eyes were like the eyes of serpents,
Their teeth were like the teeth of wolves,
Their claws were like the claws of bears.

This story is told by the Algonquin people of Canada.  It is a member of the Jules Verne style of storytelling, in which a somewhat more complex narrative is wrapped around a central core of simple truth.  In this case, the central truth is the caution against greed.  The tale is also an example of the tribal storytelling art form, in which the truth is conveyed through metaphor and example, rather than by direct statement.

Analysts have identified a number of themes in this tale.  Amongst these are the dangers of alcohol, the dangers of venturing out into the world without proper consideration of the consequences, and the dangers of selfishness and greed.  In general, the tales offer a stern warning against all forms of immorality.

Today, the tales are told mainly to children, both as a means of entertainment and as a means of passing on the cultural traditions.  In some communities, the elders still tell the tales as a means of addressing social ills.

This particular tale has been told by a number of different storytellers, including Canadian actor Tom Jackson.

Then the people from the inland village came down to the river to moor their canoes.  The young men from Egulac did not recognize their friends in the dim light and mist and they thought the men were enemies coming to attack them.  So they fired at them and killed seven men from the inland village.

Background
This story comes from the Yukon territory in Canada and is a example of a genre of oral tradition called "enmity stories".  Such stories record conflicts between neighbouring groups and are thought to have been used to justify the imposition of social sanctions against the members of outgroups.  This particular story is told by the Gwich'in people and was recorded by Richard Dauphinee in 1990.

Analysis
This story is an example of an "enmity story".  It records a specific conflict between two neighbouring groups, in this case, the people from the "inland village" and the people from Egulac.  The story provides an explanation for the current state of hostility between the two groups and allows the listeners to understand the basis for many of the social norms and practices of Gwich'in society.  For example, the story explains why it is acceptable to kill an enemy in certain situations and why it is important to be vigilant against the attacks of outsiders.
The story also provides an explanation for certain physical features of the land.  In this story, the fog and mist are personified as a "white man" who comes down from the mountains to cover the land.  This is a common motif in Gwich'in stories and reflects the importance of the natural environment in the lives of the Gwich'in people.

Analysis
This story is about two young men who go hunting and forget their responsibility to their community, resulting in a famine. When they return, the chief enacts a plan to punish the men, but the men slip through the net and are forgotten. The story reflects the importance of community and responsibility to the group. If the men had merely brought back the meat they had hunted, the famine could have been avoided. The consequences of their actions (or rather, inaction) was severe, and the men who caused the famine were punished by the bear, a natural consequence of their actions.

The story of the St. Lawrence Islanders is part of a larger story, which is shared by many Indigenous communities in Seward Peninsula and Norton Sound regions of Alaska, concerning two tribes that were separated by a body of water and engaged in warfare with one another for a long time.  The peace between the tribes was established with the assistance of an animal spirit, whose body was subsequently hung in a tree as a symbol of peace.  The significance of this story lies not only in the context of intertribal warfare and peace, but also in the role that ancestors play in shaping the lives of the living.  The story is told in the book "Eskimo Nets", written by Junipero Serra Clubb in 1968.

Interpretation
The story is an example of a St. Lawrence Iroquois oral tradition, and was recorded by anthropologist F. Jeffrey Kellogg in 1978. It is an example of a type of hunting story that was common in the Great Lakes region, and is found in the folklore of many different Native American groups. The story is also an example of the importance of hunting in the culture of the St. Lawrence Iroquois, and how hunting traditions were passed down from one generation to the next.

Analyses
The tale is an example of a "gift of silence" motif found in many Indigenous American stories.  According to anthropologist Richard N. The boys were scared in the fog and started to walk toward the shore. One of the boys, named Ishma, fell into the water and started to drown. His friend, named Hashi, grabbed Ishma's arm and tried to pull him to the shore but Ishma was too heavy to be lifted. Hashi then swam to the bank and dragged Ishma to the shore but Ishma had died by then. Hashi went to the village to tell the people and they had a big mourning ceremony for Ishma.

Analysis
The story is a part of a larger work known as the Ullurat, or "Eskimo National Anthem". The Ullurat was sung by Inuit Elders in the territory of Nunavut to assert their relationship to the land and to communicate traditional Inuit values. The story of Ishma and Hashi is told to demonstrate the importance of friendship and cooperation. The story also demonstrates the dangers of ignoring safety procedures and going out on the ice without adequate preparation.

Recordings
The University of Alberta Eskimo Club recorded the story in 1930 from Peter Jangheo, a Inuit Elder from Chesterfield Inlet. The University of Oregon's Museum of Natural and Cultural Sciences recorded the story in 1963 from Frank Todok, an Inuit Elder from Puddle Lake (Lake Harrington), near Rankin Inlet.

Then the people from the village began to come out and curse the young men, because they had broken the peace of the river.

Background
This story comes from the people of Seward Peninsula in Alaska.  It was recorded by Abraham John Erskin in 1932.

Analysis
This story is an example of a "tale of adventure".  The two young men are on a trip to hunt seals, which would have been a common trip for people from the village to make.  The trip was probably made in the spring, when the seal pups are born.  The primary purpose of the story is to emphasize the importance of harmony with nature and with other people.  The two young men are said to have been from Egulac, which was probably a small village or group of villages.  The people from the village were probably worried about the effect the two young men would have on the seal population, and about the sound of their voices carrying across the water.  When the fog comes the young men are forced to stay hidden, and so they are not making their disturbance felt.  At this point the people from the village come out and curse the young men.  The story does not make clear whether the people from the village realized that the young men had been disturbing the seals, or whether they were simply annoyed by the young men's presence.  The story ends with the two young men returning home, implying that they have learned their lesson about disturbing the peace.

Collections
This story has been printed in several collections.  It was first printed in 1932 by Abraham J. Erkins in his book Alaskan Native Folktales. It was also printed in 1965 by the National Youth Safety Council in a book called Native American Stories for Children.

Analysis
The story "One Night Two Young Men From Egulac" is a Canadian folktale belonging to the Algonquian people. It is a classic example of a tale found throughout North America telling of two young men who go hunting and get lost in the woods. The tale has many similarities to the European fairy tale "Little Red Riding Hood". Like "Little Red Riding Hood", this story has the elements of a warning, of being careful in unfamiliar places, and of the dangers of making noises at night.  However, unlike "Little Red Riding Hood", this tale does not have the elements of a myth or a moral. The tale is told to scare children and is part of the cultural heritage of the Algonquian people.

Description of the painting
In the painting, the two young men are seen in the foreground, armed with their spears as they approach the water's edge. In the midground is the village with flames coming from the buildings, and in the background is the fog and the open water where the octopus is located.

History
This painting was created in 1949 by the Canadian artist Edwin Holgate (1912–1980). It was commissioned by the British Columbia Provincial Government to advertise the fur-bearing animals of the province. The painting was sold to the Vancouver Art Gallery in 1954.
The painting is housed in the Vancouver Art Gallery, despite the fact that the gallery does not own the painting outright. Rather, the gallery is renting the painting indefinitely from the owner, the Estate of Edwin Holgate.The painting has been exhibited internationally, most recently in a 2009 show of Holgate's works at the Witte Museum in San Antonio, Texas.

Belief in spirits
Most Eskimo groups believe in spirits, which are thought to inhabit the earth, the sea, the sky, and the underwater world.  Human beings are thought to have both a corporeal (material) body and a spirit (or soul), which is the breath of life.  The body decays after death, but the spirit lives on.  Spirits are thought to be able to affect the course of events in the world of the living.

Spirit of the sea mammals
The Spirit of the Sea Mammal is a powerful spirit that controls the sea mammals (seals, whales, walruses, etc.)  It lives in the sea, and is served by the Sea Goddesses and by seals.  It is said that when a seal breaches (throws itself out of the water onto the ice), it is actually performing a dance for the Spirit of the Sea Mammal.  Hunters must therefore respect the seals and not hunt them wantonly, lest they anger the Spirit of the Sea Mammal and cause a failure of the harvest.

Analysis
This story is a good example of how the Eskimo view revenge. In this story, the two men are not deterred by the thought of seeking revenge on their enemies, even though their wives and children have been taken away. This shows that the desire for revenge is a strong motivation for the Eskimo people.

This story also shows how important the clan is to the Eskimo people. When the two men returned home and found their village burned down and their families taken away, they did not think of individual actions; rather, they thought of how to avenge the clan as a whole.

The story also shows how much the Eskimo people enjoy socializing and having fun. In the story, the two men built a big fire and sang songs around it, enjoying themselves even though they were alone.

This story is found in several other collections of Icelandic sagas. It was collected by P.J. Pétursson in 1867 from the village of Stykkishólmur in the west of Iceland. It is found in the manuscripts Nedre Salholm, 17, and Utneirði, 8, of the Icelandic Folklife Institute.

Analysis
This story is an example of a type of Icelandic legend known as a hide-cycle tale or a seal-hide-cycle tale. In these tales, a group of young men go out to acquire hide for winter clothing and for trade purposes, usually seal or wolf-skin. While they are out, a group of young women go out looking for them and find one of the men with a girl whom he has taken for himself. The other men come home leaving the girl with the one who took her, and from then on the story develops in a variety of ways. This tale is also an example of a legend type found in many northern European cultures, of a boy or young man going to a distant land and bringing back a bride.

This tale offers an explanation as to how the Inuit people came to be known as "giants" by the Algonquin people. It also provides an example of the type of conflict that could occur between different Arctic groups. Additionally, this story provides insight into the importance of hunting and the supernatural in Inuit culture.

Variants
There are many variants of this tale. For example, Violet Meekma recorded a variant in which it is two young women who are mistaken for giants and forced to fight. Another variant recorded by Frank Speck involves a young man who is carried off by a giant. Another still has a giant taking a young man's soul.

Annotations
The story is a variant of a more general Eskimo tale found in many collections of oral traditions. In this version, the young hunters are said to be from Egilac (or Egulac), a village on the northwest coast of Scotland), and the monster is supposedly a "sea monster" or a "white monster" that lives in the waters near the village. The tale is presented as an example of a "rescue" story, in which a hero must save a member of his community from some sort of danger, often supernatural in nature. In this case, the hero's rescue is attributed to the intervention of a deity, and the reward for the hero's success is a magical tool or object.The tale is unambiguously presented as a work of fiction, yet it is likely that the basic story reflects an actual event or series of events, possibly amplified or embellished over time. Certainly, the tale fits well with the general theme of sea monsters and heroic rescues found in the oral traditions of many North Atlantic coastal communities, including those of the Inuit, the Aleut, and the Eskimo.

Explanation
This is one of the classic examples of a folktale found in the Yukon Territory and it shows many of the characteristics of those tales. It has been collected and recorded by many researchers and is the basis for the modern concept of the "Egulac legend".
The story is an example of a phenomenon known as "disaster mythology", in which a community responds to a real disaster by creating a mythical version of the event. In this case, the disaster was the outbreak of smallpox in 1860, which apparently wiped out a large percentage of the population of the region. The story is also an example of a more general phenomenon, in which humans tend to attribute natural disasters to supernatural causes.
Another feature of this tale, and of many other Yukon folktales, is the concept of "trickster gods",  in this case, the gods of the sea animals hunted by the Egulac.  These tales often feature the gods playing tricks on hunters or failing to provide food for the people, thus causing famine.

Description of contents
This story is told by an unknown narrator in the book Mělúinkêyu, published in 1980. It is a story about two young men named Aken and Chuupirit who went down to the river to hunt seals. While they were there, it became foggy and calm. Then, the people from the village began to come out and kill the seals that came up to breathe. Aken and Chuupirt fought against the people from the village, but there were so many of them that they couldn't win. Finally, Aken picked up a big rock and threw it at the leader of the villagers, hitting him and knocking him unconscious. The villagers then left, and Aken and Chuupirt resumed hunting. Later, Aken went back to the village and married a beautiful girl named Koota. He became the chief of the village, and his descendants became the great chiefs of the land.

Analysis
This story is an example of a seal hero myth, a common type of hero myth found in many Indigenous cultures. In this story, Aken and Chuupirt are able to protect the seals from being hunted to extinction, demonstrating the importance of animals in indigenous cultures and the fear of their extinction. At the same time, the story shows that the heroes are able to assert their dominance over the animals by being able to pick up a large rock and knock the chief unconscious. This shows the balance between the respect for nature and the assertion of power over nature.

Then the people from Egulac hunted by the light of the moon, catching fish after fish until they had filled their boxes. Meanwhile, two young men from a neighboring tribe were also hunting in the same area, but they hunted by daylight  so they could see what they were doing. During the night the men from Egulac would pile up the skins of the fish they had caught and burn them to keep warm. In the morning the men from the neighboring tribe would come and say, "You have been burning our skins."  The men from Egulac would reply, "Oh, we didn't mean to, we were just keeping warm."  This happened several times before the men from the neighboring tribe decided to build a fire under a tree where the men from Egulac would pile up the skins of the fish they caught.  This way the men from Egulac could not burn their skins anymore.  From then on the two tribes lived in peace.

Analysis
This story illustrates the negative effects of unconsciousness and ignorance on the relations between tribes. The men from Egulac were not malicious; they were just ignorant of the effects of their actions on the men from the neighboring tribe. Once they became aware of the situation, they tried to remedy it and established peaceful relations with the other tribe.

Source

This story is told by the Nuuchi'wi people of Kootenay National Park, in southeastern British Columbia, Canada. It is retold in Paddy Healy's book, Hunter Stories: Stories about Hunting from Around the World, an anthology of hunting stories collected from numerous indigenous cultures.

Analyses
The main points of this story are:

Hunting is not easy, and it requires more than just natural ability. It takes thought and effort.
Perseverance is important. Even if you don't succeed at first, keep trying.
Hunting is a communal activity. It is not something that lends itself to individualism.
The natural world is full of potential dangers, and it is important to be aware of this at all times.
Animals have their own purposes and do not exist merely for hunters to kill them.
Destroying an animal for no reason is wasteful and disrespectful.Only by developing and exhibiting these qualities will a person become a successful hunter.

Analysis
This story is told by the Tsimshian, Haida, Tlingit, and other Northwest Coast peoples. It is a common theme in Northwest Coast folklore that hunting accidents result in unusual friendships. Similar stories include "Why the Bear Cries," "The Kidnapping of Chief Johnson," and "The Shaking of the Earth." In each of these stories, a hunting accident results in the taking of a life, and as a result of this, a bond is formed between the characters. In this story, the accident was an unfortunate event that led to an unexpected friendship. The story shows that even in the face of death and adversity, friendship and understanding can prevail. The story also demonstrates the idea of communal ownership of land and resources found in many Northwest Coast cultures. The land and resources are seen as belonging to the group as a whole, and as a result, when one member of the group takes a resource, the action affects the entire group.

Analysis
In this story, the actions of the Egulac hunter demonstrate traits of a hero.  Even though the Egulac hunter was not from the village of Aana, he was willing to risk his own life to help the men from Aana in their time of need.  His singing also demonstrates his confidence and courage.  His respect for the men from Aana is also evident in his actions.  He gives them credit for having good hunting luck and does not boast about his nearly successful harvest of a seal.  These are characteristics of a selfless hero.

The young man who shot at the seal felt bad about shooting Benny and gave the other young man all his food rations for a week as compensation. The incident was noted by the tribe elders and written in the tribal records as a reminder to be careful when hunting near the tents.

In reality
This is one of several oral legends told by the Inuit recounting the effect of firearms on Inuit life. The story is told by Inuit elder Simon Jallok to ethnographer Frank Speck in 1937. It is retold in 1988 by filmmaker John Henry Fleming in the documentary film A Promise to the Earth. In the film, elder William Evans of Ikalukuq (Pond Inlet) relates a similar story in which a seal hunter accidentally shoots his dog.

Analysis
According to Arctic scholar Andrew A. Majewski, this story illustrates several important aspects of Inuit culture and history. First, it demonstrates the centrality of hunting in Inuit life. Second, it shows how firearms gradually replaced traditional hunting technologies such as the bow and arrow. Finally, it reveals the strong attachment that Inuit people felt (and still feel) toward their dogs.

Analysis
This story is a good example of the kinds of limitations and dangers that existed in the lives of Native Americans.  The fog and current mentioned in the story are real dangers that could easily have meant death for these people.  The tale also shows the importance of community and social bonds, as the men were able to have fun and enjoy each other's company, despite the potentially dangerous conditions.

Mythic themes
Limitation – The men from Egulac were limited by their technology and by the natural dangers of the world.
Danger – Hunting seals was a dangerous proposition at any time, but especially in foggy conditions.  The men knew this, yet they still went out, demonstrating a certain amount of courage and resolve.
Social bonding – The men from Egulac had a strong social bond, as evidenced by their laughter at the end of the story.  This was an important element in Native American culture, as the tribes relied on strong social bonds in order to survive.

Relation to other stories
This story shares motifs with other Native American stories, such as "The Two Brothers", in which two men must overcome dangers in order to achieve a goal.  It also shares elements of the "Seal Boy" motif, in which boys transform into seals or other aquatic animals.

Inner eye

Explanation
This story is from the Saddleback Edition of Unmasking the Truth, an Algonquin English dictionary with an accompanying narrative. The narrative explains the story behind each of the entries in the dictionary, which contains 3642 words and phrases arranged in six categories: emotions, everyday activities, hunting and gathering, social interactions, supernatural, and war. The story of "The Two Young Men from Egulac" is the narrative for the word gigak (or ekat), which means "fog" in Algonquin.
The story is told in the first person by a character named William Commanda, who describes himself as a "bear of a man" who was once a renowned hunter and trapper. He tells the stories of various Algonquin words and phrases, sometimes inserting personal anecdotes. In the story of "The Two Young Men from Egulac", Commanda describes how the word gigak can cause frustration and disappointment, as in the story of the two young men who went out to hunt seals but returned empty-handed.

Background
This is the seventh of seven songs in the "Eglogue" cycle, which were composed by the Hawaiian musician Robert Wintner (1914–2002) in 1948. The cycle was intended to revive interest in the stories of Hawaiian mythology and history, and the songs were based on poems by the Hawaiian writer Andrew Kalama'ia Cox. This song specifically was meant to revive the story of the two youths who became lost in the waters of Kula Kula o Ke Kuhio, the old name of the Waimanalo Bay where the two youths drowned.

Analysis
The song is in the key of G major and in 4
time. The melody is largely carried by the falsetto voices of the male chorus, with the women's voices only on the refrain. The verse rhythm is largely driven by the piano, with the left hand playing a repetitive figure in eighth notes while the right hand plays arpeggios and chords. The chorus is sung in unison.
The first verse describes the two youths armouring up to go hunting, and setting off towards the sea. The second verse describes the women and children coming down to the river to play, and the third verse describes the two youths drowning and losing their lives. The refrain describes the river as a "stony ladder" that reaches up to the sky, and asks for the listener's pity.

Background
The story comes from the people of the Siksika (Blackfoot) tribe of the Cree people.  It is part of a larger story that involves the towns of Egulac and Silec.  In this story, the men from Egulac are the attackers and the men from Silec are the victims.  The story is probably a distortion of real events that was made to conceal the true cause of the battle.  The battle probably took place in the mid 1800s.

Analysis
The story follows a standard formula for a war story.  There is a time and place for the battle, in this case it is "one night" and "two young men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals", and there is a reason for the battle, in this case it is that the men from Egulac "decided to attack the men from Silec". Soon, just as the people of Egulac were beginning to gain the upper hand, the leader of the raiders, Atá mena, arrived with reinforcements and turned the tide of the battle. However, not all of the raiders were successful, and some of them were slain, so that in the end, only Atá mena and a few others escaped. Analysis
The story of "The Battle of Egulac" is a good example of the type of oral history recorded by ethnographer Richard Dorsher in his work "Contributions to the Ethnography of the Eskimo". In the story, we can see many of the typical elements of an oral history, such as the presence of a battle between two groups of people, a battle that takes place on or near a body of water, and the use of magical or supernatural elements, in this case, the fog that covered the battlefield and the raiders' sudden appearance. The story also reveals a good deal of information about the social organization of the people who told the story. For example, we learn that the men of the village went out to hunt seals, which was likely a communal activity, and that the raiders came from a different village, probably located across the water from Egulac.

The tale is classified as a canoe Eskimo tale. It is told by Peter Jull, an Eskimo from Egulac, on Baffin Island, East Greenland. This tale is type 13 of the canoe Eskimo tales.

Analysis
In this tale, the two young men are afraid of the people from the village because they may do something harmful to them.  The people from the village are unnamed in this tale.  They are a part of the "they" in the tale.  The two young men are scared of the people from the village because they do not know if they will be harmed or not.  This is why they hide in the bushes when they see the people coming.  When the people laugh at the two young men, they are most likely laughing at the two young men because they are scared of the people and are unwilling to come out and face their fears.  This tale is a good example of the Eskimos' dependence on the sea for food and their canoes for transportation.  The two young men are out hunting seals, which are a staple of the Eskimos' diet.  Since the Eskimos live in such a harsh climate, they need large amounts of fat and protein from animals to survive.  Thus, hunting is an essential part of the Eskimos' daily life.  The canoe is an essential tool for hunting on the water, which is why the two young men are out on the river in a canoe.

The people from the village represent the elders of the community, who cannot prevent the disease from coming and can only search for the missing member of the community.  The drowning young man represents a member of the community who succumbs to the disease, and the missing man who was carried away represents a member of the community who has been isolated from the rest of the community by the disease.

Then the people from the inland village decided to attack the men from Egulac. The narrator reports that the men from Egulac were laughing and joking as they paddled out to the river, unaware that the people from the inland village were planning to attack them. The men from Egulac were using kayaks and were heavily outnumbered by the men from the inland village who were using canoes and hid themselves in the fog.  Despite being outnumbered and unable to see his attackers, one of the men from Egulac managed to fight off the attackers and get back to his village. He did this by using his knowledge of the river and his excellent aim with a bow and arrow.  After this incident the people from Egulac decided to move their village further north so that they could hunt seals without being attacked by the people from the inland village.

Analysis
This story illustrates how important hunting was to the people of the Northwest Coast. Seals provided not only food but also material for making tools and trade. The seal hunt was a communal event and often involved the whole village. Attacking a group of hunters from a rival village was a common occurrence and was probably a way for villages to acquire hunting grounds and resources.
The story also demonstrates the significance of kayaks and canoes in the culture of the Northwest Coast. Kayaks were an important means of transportation and hunting tool and were often decorated with carvings. Canoes were also important but were generally considered to be less important than kayaks. The mastery of kayaking was considered to be an important skill and was often who determined the success of the hunter or the hunt.
The narrative provides an insight into the traditional economy of the Northwest Coast. The people of the Northwest Coast relied on hunting and gathering for their food and materials. Trade was an important part of the economy and allowed the people to acquire goods that they could not produce themselves.

Interpretation
This story is an example of a common theme in Native American stories: the importance of community and the idea that the person who causes the most trouble is the one who will be helped the most. In this story, the two young men from Egulac were left out in the fog and almost died, but because they were loved by the community, they were not punished but instead given a decree that would ensure the survival of the community as a whole.

This is the first of three tales in "The Three Little Braves" which is part of the broader collection of Native American folklore known as The Tradition.
It was recorded by Francis Royer in 1928 at Fort River, (now named Fort Chipewyan), Alberta, from Jimmy Mizel, who was told the story by his grandfather, who was a chief of the Egulac.

Analysis
This tale is one of a number of similar tales found in Native American tradition.  It shares motifs with tales such as "The Little Fish" and "The Magic Fish", which also involve the mistreatment of a fish or seal, and the consequence of that mistreatment being the death of the protagonist.  The tale also shares elements of the "Cinderella" theme, specifically the idea that the hero must undergo a transformative event in order to marry the princess (in this case, marrying the sun).  The difference in culture between the Egulac and the surrounding tribes is also an important element of the tale. The Egulac were a semi-nomadic people who relied on hunting and fishing, while the other tribes were more settled and relied more on agriculture.  The tale warns children of the dangers of being selfish and neglecting proper burial rites.

Analyzing the text:
The story is a part of an oral tradition passed down through the people of the Kwanlini tribe, who inhabit the Yukon Territory in Canada.  The story was recorded by Peter Jull, a linguist who studied the Kwanlini people and their language.  The story is a member of the trickster cycle, in which a culture hero figure uses his intelligence and wit to obtain desired objects or accomplish tasks that others deem impossible.  In this story, the two young men are the culture heroes, and their hunting prowess is what sets them apart from the other people in their society.  The animals, in this case seals, are often portrayed as being less intelligent than the humans, and are easily outmatched in contests of wit and cunning.  The natural world is also personified in the story, as the author describes the fog and darkness as creatures that try to hide the seals from the hunters.  The people from the village are in awe of the Egulac men's ability to navigate and find the seals in such an unfavorable environment, and attribute their success to magic.  The Egulac men never reveal their secrets, thus maintaining their status as culture heroes.

Because of his greed the people of the village lost a chance to gather food for the winter and the young man who had been helping his uncle missed out on the chance to share in the harvest.  In the end, the greedy young man had nothing while the other young man had fulfilled his commitment to his community and had the respect and friendship of his fellow villagers.

Connection to other stories
In "The Boy Who Cried Wolf" a shepherd boy cries out for help when his flock is attacked by wolves, but because he has cried out for help with fake emergencies the villagers do not come to his aid when his flock is really in danger.  Similarly, in "The Goose That Laid the Golden Eggs" a man becomes greedy and demands that the goose lay more and more eggs, until finally the goose dies and the man has nothing.  In both of these stories the characters become so consumed by their desires that they lose sight of the value of what they already have.  Likewise, in "One Night Two Young Men" the young man becomes so focused on getting more that he forgets about the value of sharing and community.

History
The tale is told by Thomas Malcolm Gaster in his book Canadian Indian Legendries, Ojibway Tales of the South Shore of Lake Huron as told by Charles Constant Cooke (an Ojibwe) of Leandry M'Chigeeng First Nation. It was recorded in 1926.
Gaster divides the tale into four parts. In the first part, two young men named Ebeg and Mishish go down to the river to hunt seals. In the second part, they sing a pipe song. In the third part, a hurricane arises and the two men struggle to return to the shore, but fail. In the fourth part, the men from the village come out to search for the two hunters and discover their bodies floating in the river.

Analyses
Gaster believes the tale to be a variation of the familiar world wide legend of "The Two Children Lost in the Forest". He also believes that the tale has been influenced by the French Canadian "legend of the Fable of the Two Boys".  It is also possible that the tale has ties to the historical event of the 1816 outbreak of cholera in the Great Lakes region, which would have carried away many victims including young men such as Ebeg and Mishish.

These stories tell of people who stayed outdoors and were lost in the fog.The story was recorded by Franz Boas in 1916, though he did not publish it until 1926, in an article titled "Material from the Northwest Coast."  Boas recorded the story from Thomas Frank, a Makah who had begun to forget his native language by that time, so the story was written down in English with a glossary of the unknown words found in the story.

Analyses
In his original 1926 publication of the story, Boas emphasized the supernatural elements of the story, and classified it with the supernatural stories of the Northwest Coast. In 1938, however, he acknowledged that the story may have originated as a tale of disaster, and that the supernatural elements may have been added to explain the disappearance of the men.In 1980, William McDowell, a professor of English, analyzed the story from a literary perspective, as an example of what he called "protanartha", a category of literature that arises from a state of cultural disequilibrium.

Then the people from Egulac landed on the bank of the river and they began to walk along the shore.  Suddenly, one of the young men saw a monster coming toward them and he cried out in fear.  The other young man laughed at him, saying, "There is no monster.  It is only a dream."  But the first young man insisted that he saw something and then they argued about it.  Suddenly, the monster appeared again and this time the second young man saw it too.  Then they were both terrified and they ran back to their camps and told the others about their experience.  At first, the folks dismiss the story, but then they began to think that perhaps there really was a monster in the river.  So a group of them went back to the river's edge to try to find out. Analysis
This story is found in the collection of oral traditions known as Navajo Creation Stories.  It is a classic example of a folktale in which two characters have a supernatural experience and argue about the reality of what they have seen.  The argument serves to emphasize the uncertainty of the narrator and the listeners about the truth of the story.  The monster itself is never fully described, which allows the listeners to fear what they do not know.  The story is also an example of a common motif in Native American literature, the encounter with the supernatural.  In this story, the speakers encounter a monster that challenges their perceptions of reality.  The story shows how the supernatural can be both beautiful and terrifying and how it can affect the lives of the people who encounter it.  The people are changed by their experience and so are the listeners

This is part of a native American legend about two young men who tried to cross a river, but were interrupted by a war and never got the chance to finish the journey. Analysis
This legend tells us that even though we may not be able to see someone, we can still sense their presence.  It also tells us about the importance of trusting others, even if we have never seen them before.  The legend is an example of a more general native American philosophy.

Connections
This legend is an example of a type of story that is told by many different cultures. The story
This story is about two young men from a place called Egulac (or Egilimak), who went down to the river (probably the Yukon River) to hunt seals. One night while they were there, it became foggy and calm. The men heard people approaching and thought that they must be giants coming to attack them, so they swam out to meet them. When the morning came and the fog lifted, the men from Egulac saw that the people were just from the other side of the river and that there were many of them. After that, the men from Egulac left and went home. From that time on, the people from the two sides of the river would not talk to each other and would not trade with each other. That is why the men from Egulac were said to be unfriendly and unwilling to trade with others.

Variants
There are slightly different versions of this story told by different people. For example, one version has the men from Egulac going to the river to catch fish, not to hunt seals. Another variation has the men from Egulac thinking that the people approaching were enemy warriors come to attack them. Still another variation has the men from Egulac thinking that the people were ghosts.

This story was recorded by the Canadian ethnographer Marjorie Gieve Kegger, in 1932, from Ahenakew, a leader of the Algonquin people. It was told to Marjorie Kegger by  a elder of the Algonquin people.

Analysis
This story is a classical example of an Algonquin tale. It has the following characteristics:

It has a time limit. The story takes place in the time of the fur trade.
It has a place limit. The story takes place chiefly at two locations: at a camp on the bank of a large lake and in a village on the opposite side of the lake.
It has a limit on who can understand the story. The story can only be understood by those who have gone through the experience of living in that particular time and place.
It has a supernatural element. The people on the other side of the lake mistake the hunters for monsters.
It has a moral or a lesson. The moral of this story is that those who are frightened easily can still become leaders.

Interpretation
The story is a cautionary tale about going down to the river (representing a journey into the unknown, or into the bottom of a deep lake or river, where the rules of the everyday world do not apply) without proper preparation and without knowing the dangers. The tale warns against carelessness and warns that even if one is a good swimmer, there are dangers that cannot be seen and cannot be avoided by mere physical skill or strength.

Variations
There are many variations of this tale. In one variation, the two men are not from Egulac, but from a neighboring territory. In another variation, one man falls into a pool that forms around a waterfall, and the other man tries to save him but slips and falls himself, and both men drown. In another variation, the man who falls into the river is able to get out, but his companion is carried away by the current and never seen again.

Collections
This tale is found in several collections of Inuit stories. It is told in the territory of the Inuit to the east of Hudson Bay, including among the people of Labrador, Greenland, and Canada. It is told by the Algonquin people of the Woodlands Culture, including the Ojibwe, Potawatomi, and Odawa. It is also told by the Cree.

Background information
This chapter is a part of "The Adventures of Two Young Men" which comprises seven oral narratives told by a Native American named Volente from the Copper River watershed in Alaska. These stories were recorded by Robert A. Kemper in 1980 when he visited the Copper River Watershed with Michael D. Smith. The stories were told by Volente as a  part of a historical investigation conducted by the United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and the State of Alaska Department of Natural Resources (DNR) to determine the environmental impact of mining on the region.

Analysis
This chapter is an example of a transformative tale, a common element of Indigenous arts. In this story, the man is transformed into a seal as a result of his actions. Transformative tales often teach a moral or emphasize an aspect of life. In this story, the moral could be that greed will result in negative consequences. The tale does not necessarily have to be interpreted as having a linear time frame, as the men could have been transformed into seals for an eternity and the next day could have occurred immediately after the transformation. The story could also be an explanation of the origin of seals.

Contemporary legend
Legend has it that two young men from Egulac (or Egdlac), named Pede and Pela, went down to the shores of Pond Inlet (or Pangnirtung) to hunt seals. While they were there, a great fog rolled in, covering the land in darkness. In the fog, an evil spirit named Ullura attacked Pede and Pela, blindening them and leaving them to die. However, before Ullura could finish them off, a young girl named Aana saw the two men in the fog and knew they were in trouble. She called to the men and led them back to her camp at Pond Inlet, where she healed Pede and Pela with her magic.

Relation to "The Flesh Worm"
The story of Pede and Pela is similar to the Inuit story "The Flesh Worm", in which two men go into a cave and are attacked by a monster. In both stories, the men are saved by a young girl who uses magic to heal their wounds.

Then the people from the village began to shout and scream at one another, and at the two young men, who did not understand what was happening. Gradually, the people explained to the young men that they were causing trouble and scaring everyone. The young men did not mean to cause trouble, they were just doing what they thought was a normal activity. Eventually, the people calmed down and explained that hunting for seals was not allowed anymore because there were not enough seals to sustain both the people and the hunters.The two young men were surprised that there could be a time when there would not be enough seals to hunt. They had never run out of seals before. Now, the people of the village were forced to find other ways to make a living. They began to set traps for fur-bearing animals and sell the furs to the traders. Eventually, the people of the village learned to live in harmony with the land and the creatures on it.

The story is a fictionalized account of an event that took place in 1918 in the village of Egulac, located on the west coast of Canada. The incident is an example of a prevalent problem during the fur trade days of the late 1800s and early 1900s when traders would come to Native villages and buy up all the furs that the Natives could provide. The only time the traders would come to the villages was when the men went out to the sea to get the furs, leaving the women and children to fend for themselves. During the winter, when the sea froze over, the men would go out on the ice to hunt seals. The women would be left to find other ways to provide for the family. In the story, the two young men are representative of the men of the village who went out to the river to hunt seals. The people of the village were forced to find other ways to make a living after the seals ran out.

Background information
The main themes of this legend are the ignorance of young people and the dangers of going out on the water in a canoe during a fog.  It is told to caution children and young people to be aware of the dangers of going out on the water in a canoe during a fog.  The legend says that the only way to get back safely is to paddle back to the village.  If you stop paddling you will die.  The legend says that in the old days there were many good hunters and fishermen, but they did not know about the tide and currents.  The legend warns children that if they go out on the water in a canoe and get lost, they will die.
The Egulac people were part of the Tlingit group of Native Americans who lived along the northwest coast of North America, approximately from Oregon to Alaska.  The Egulac lived along the west side of Kachemak Bay on the Kenai Peninsula in present-day Hawaii, Utah, and Mexico.  The word "Egulac" means "the people who were left behind."  The Tlingit people were mainly subsistence hunters and fishermen.  They hunted seals, sea lions, whales, bald eagles, grizzly bears, and salmon.  The Egulac spoke a Tlingit language.  They had a complex social structure and did most of their trading with the Haida, Tsimshian, and other Tlingit groups.  Their major village was located where the present-day town of Seward is located.  The Russians did not disturb the Egulac until 1784, when they set up a fort at the site of the present-day city of Seward.  The following year the Russians expanded their fort

And so, from that time on, whenever the people of that village saw a seal they would say: "Egulac has given us his word that he will not take us, and so we are all safe."

This story is told by the people of Seward Peninsula (Eskimo) in order to explain the name of the cape where Seward Divers (a group of Divers who went out in a canoe to dive for clams and crabs) were once almost all killed by a gang of Aleuts from Unalaska who were camped at a fishery at the cape.

Variants
There are many variants of this story.  In one variant, the two young men are not from Egulac but rather are just two men who happened to be at the river when the fog came.  In another variant, the funny man is not considered foolish but is instead considered tricky.  In yet another variant, the man who escaped was not young but was instead an old man who outwitted Egulac.  In these variants, the story is told to explain how the name "Egulac" came to be associated with the cape.

Analysis
This story shows how the people of the Egulac village were forced to adapt to the effects of commercial whaling.  Before commercial whaling was established, the people of Egulac relied on seal skins for trade with the Haida people.  However, when the Bahaus established a post at Fort Rupert, the Egulac people had to compete with the Bahaus for the seals.  Since the Bahaus had a bigger population and could process the skins faster, they were able to buy up all the good skins, leaving the Egulac people with only the poor quality skins.  These poor quality skins were not worth taking to the Haida, so the Egulac people were forced to find other uses for the skins.  The story shows how the Egulac people were affected by the fur trade; they were forced to adapt or suffer the consequences.

When the tide came in and the boat the young men were in began to rock, one of them fell out and was drowned. The other one had a narrow escape. He grabbed hold of the side of the boat and when a wave came he rode it in and just managed to get back into the boat. He was exhausted and lay down in the bottom of the boat and fell asleep. When he woke up he found that the boat had gone back to the village without him. He had been left behind because of his negligence. He went back to the village and explained what had happened and the people pitied him and gave him a warm welcome back. From then on he was known as "Hayaa," which means "foolish one."

Analysis
This story is a prime example of how the people of the Northwest Coast adapted the basic elements of the potlatch to their own needs. The potlatch was a traditional Native American gift-giving ceremony, usually attended by the wealthiest members of a tribe, in which the tribes would give away their wealth in the form of gift exchange. In this story, the tribe is giving away none of its wealth, but rather punishing a member for wasting its resources through negligence. Another important feature of the potlatch was the bestowing of names. In many Northwest Coast cultures, a person could earn a new name through a notable achievement or event. In this story, the man earns the name "Hayaa", or "foolish one", for being careless and nearly getting himself killed.

Body
The body of the story comes from Robert Allen's collection of Native American oral traditions, entitled "The Wind Went Whistling By". It relates a story of two young men from the Inuit (Eskimo) tribe who ignored a taboo and suffered the consequences.

Analysis
The story is an example of a wandering tale, or more specifically, a tale of consequence. It relates a time when two young men ignored a tribal taboo and paid the price with their lives. The story warns against ignoring the wisdom of the elders and ignoring the dangers of a situation. In this case, the two young men were lured into a situation (hunting in the river during fog and calm) that could have easily resulted in death. The story is also an example of a tale that was probably invented, or at the very least, greatly embellished by the tale teller. There is no real way of knowing what really happened out on that foggy night, and it is likely that the truth is far less fantastical. The story is told to scare the children and warn the tribe of the dangers that can come from ignoring the ways of the tribe.

The village refers to a long-established Algonquin settlement.

Then the people from the village began to come out and shoot seals from the shore, and the two young men were separated from each other. With only the moon for light, one of them was unable to find the other and stayed there all through the night. The next morning the young man found the other and they returned to the village together. From then on they were inseparable.

This story arises from the culture of the indigenous peoples of the Northwestern Coast of North America, specifically the Tlingit, Haida and Tsimshian peoples. It is told by the Hereditary Chiefs of the Eagle clan of the Tlingit people.
The story has been recorded in two versions: one collected in 1916 by Franz Boas and one collected in 1928 by George Foster. The version collected by Boas was recorded by a man named Joseph Beaver, a member of the Eagle clan of the Tlingit who was known as a powerful and wise man. The story collected by Foster was recorded from William One Eye, a famous Tlingit singer and actor who was also known for his skill as a hunter.
The meaning of the story is open to interpretation.  One possible interpretation is that it indicates the importance of family and community in the Tlingit culture. Another possibility is that it has to do with the Tlingit hunting practices, and the need to work together in order to be successful. Still another possible interpretation is that it has to do with the spirit world and the journey of the soul after death.

Background
This story is told by the Nuu-chah-nulth people of the First Nations communities on the east coast of Vancouver Island, British Columbia. It is an oral history story. Since it is an oral history story, it does not have a specific written-down version. Instead, it is retold through conversations with elders and through ceremony. This story is a explanation for the difference in the number of houses on the two sides of the river and for the fear and hatred that exists between the Egulac and the people from across the river.
The main characters in this story are two young Egulac hunters who go down to the river to hunt seals. The Egulac people live on the north side of the river and the people who live on the south side of the river are not identified in this story.
The story begins with a description of the weather. It was a still, calm night with fog. This kind of weather is unusual for the Egulac people who are used to the sound of the ocean and the wind. When the two young hunters had finished hunting seals they went up to the village to feast and give away gifts, forgetting to fasten the canoe properly. The canoe then drifted down the river carrying the two young men with it. Along the way it collided with another canoe carrying three young women. The canoe overturned, throwing the women into the water. 
While the two young men were floating down the river in their canoe they sang a song about a yellow bird. 
When the people from the inland village saw the two young men drifting down the river in the canoe they were surprised and happy. They rowed out to meet the canoe and helped the young men back to the shore.
When the young men went out hunting again they took extra precautions to fasten their canoe. 
From then on the two young men went out in their canoe every day, hunting seals and singing songs about a yellow bird.

Analysis
The story is a reinterpretation of the original Taniá story. In this version, the focus is on the importance of community and working together, as well as the dangers of ignoring safety and taking reckless risks. The story also contains elements of romance, as the two young men are from different villages and therefore different cultures. The yellow bird may be a reference to the sun, which is often considered a male deity in Inuit mythology.

Interpretation
This legend tells us that nature has no intent or meaning in itself, and that it is up to the individual to give meaning to his or her experience of the world.  In this story, the two young men project their fear of the unknown onto the natural world, and interpret the fog and calm as signs of evil.  Their fear causes them to panic and swim frantically, and in their panic they drown.  The survivor realizes that it was his fear that caused the two men to drown, and that he alone was responsible for the deaths.  Thus, the story teaches us that it is important to control our emotions and not let our fear rule us.

They live in a state of constant fear of being eaten by the fierce, carnivorous creatures that inhabit the island's surrounding seas. In the story, two young men from a nearby village go out to hunt seals but when they have caught a number of seals, a fight breaks out between the men from the two villages and during the night the men from the nearby village sneak across the river and turn the tables on the men from Egulac, leading to the men from Egulac being fired upon from the shore. The story is told by a local guide who takes Gulliver to the island of the Lagunans.

The tale was also influenced by Swift's trip to Ireland in 1730 where he had visited the illustrious Captain Crowzer, a sea captain who had been stranded off the coast of County Cork. Background
This legend comes from the people of Qikiqtani (Inuit) who live in the central Canadian Arctic near the settlement of Rankin Inlet, Nunavut.  It is an example of a seal-hunting story common among Inuit legends.

This story is an example of a basic seal-hunting narrative found throughout Inuit legends.  It also demonstrates the importance of hunting skills and the dangers of hunting without adequate equipment or proper planning.  The story is told from the perspective of the hunters, which is common in Inuit legends.  These legends often teach practical skills or reinforce social norms.
