Background
This story is from the people of Egulac, who lived in what is now Hebron, on the east coast of Northern Sudan, near the modern day port of El Fasher. It is told by the older people of the village and is repeated by the children as a warning not to go out in canoes during a fog.

Analysis
This tale is an example of a more general folktale type found throughout the world: "The Foolish Wanderers who Refuse to Return Home".  Its central point is the importance of heeding the advice of elders and the dangers of pride and disregard for traditional customs. In this tale, the two young men are seen as foolish for refusing to return home when warned not to go out, and for disregarding the knowledge and advice of their elders. The tale punishes the two men by having them drown, thereby emphasizing the potential for disaster that results from ignoring tradition.

Variants
A similar story is told by the Mariana Islanders of the Northern Mariana Islands (Micronesia) about two young men who went out to hunt nights and ignored the warnings of the older men of the group, and a story of a young man who ignored the warnings of his father and went out in a canoe during a time of rough seas and capsize, resulting in his death.

The two hunters kept shooting at each other until both were wounded and exhausted. Finally, in the morning light, the two men saw each other and were surprised to realize that they were relatives. They apologized to each other and made up.From this story, the meaning is that people should be careful not to jump to conclusions, as there may be more to a situation than first appears.

Background
This story is from the Piteha, or "olden times," and was told by Piteha people in the Kamchatka Peninsula of Russia. It was recorded by folklorist Victor L. Shebija in 1998.

Analysis
In this story, two hunters are mistakenly led to believe that the other has killed a seal, and as a result, they engage in a shooting match that leaves both of them wounded. It was once common for people to accidentally encounter relatives while traveling, and this story serves as a reminder not to jump to conclusions about who one is shooting at. The story also demonstrates the importance of apologizing and making amends for one's actions.

Variants
A similar story, "The Shooting," is told among the Nivkh people of Siberia. In this story, a Siberian man named Yevgeny shoots at a deer and misses, and then mistakes another man, whom he had been competing with to see who could drink more alcohol, for the person who took his deer. He draws his gun and nearly shoots his friend before realizing his mistake and apologizing.

This story is an example of a common theme in Native American stories: the transformation of a human being into an animal or supernatural being as a punishment for disobeying rules or for being careless. The importance of bear in the cultures of the Native Americans
Bears are an important species in the cultures of many Native American tribes. Bears are often seen as having spiritual significance and are represented in the tales and art of many tribes. Grizzly bears are usually considered to be sacred and are rarely hunted. Bears are a staple of many Native American diets and are hunted for their meat. Salmon meals are often accompanied by bear meat. Bear fat is also highly valued. It is used as a medicine for sore eyes, inflamed tissues, and frostbite. Bear grease is also used as a waterproof coating for canoes and other watercraft.

Context
This story is told by Dauug (David) Pioeyeye, a Maori from Egulac (Egwood) on the East Coast of the North Island of New Zealand. It was collected by Elisabeth Malcolm in 1920.
It is one of several stories that were collected by Elisabeth Malcolm in the Egulac area in 1920.  These stories were recorded in order to revive the interest of the younger generation in the traditional stories of the Maori.  At the time this story was collected, the people of the Egulac district were shifting from a largely oral culture to a culture based on written information.  The younger generation preferred to hear stories about cowboys and Indians to the traditional Maori stories.  The stories collected by Elisabeth Malcolm were written down and published in a book.  The book was titled Nag the Clever Little Girl and was published in 1925.  The stories in the book were presented in a way that connected the traditional stories to the modern world.  The stories were illustrated by Emily Arlene Leist.  The original Maori versions of the stories were preserved in the Margaret Turner Collection at the National Library of New Zealand.

The tale
This tale is told by the Nuu-chah-nulth people of Clayoquat Sound, on the west coast of Vancouver Island.  It was recorded by Frank Isaac, a prominent Nuu-chah-nulth elder, in 1976.
This tale is an example of a type of story that is told by many Native American groups.  These stories are called "origin stories" or "creation stories".  They tell about how the world and the various creatures in it came into existence.  This particular story says a lot about the relationship between the Nuu-chah-nulth people and the sea.  The sea is a primary source of food and therefore an important part of Nuu-chah-nulth culture.  The story says that the people from Egulac were out hunting for food and therefore were not paying attention to their surroundings.  Because of this, they mistakenly killed two of their own people.  These types of stories are told to explain why certain things are the way they are and to teach younger members of the tribe about the importance of being aware of their surroundings and treating all living things with respect.

Analysis
This myth can be analyzed by looking at the elements that make it a classic example of a folktale. The two young men ignite the fear of the unknown, demonstrating courage in the face of the unknown, and then suffering the consequences of that fear.  The spirits of the sea are supernatural beings that have the power to change the physical world, and punish those who disturb them.  The villagers have a specific taboo against breaking, but the two hunters ignore this taboo, demonstrating a common theme found in many folktales, ignoring the advice of elders and/or taboos.  The consequences of the two hunters' actions are severe, but they learn a valuable lesson about respecting the natural world and the supernatural beings that control it.

The story of "The Two Young Men from Egulac" is a traditional Nuuchi (Nuxalk) tale from the Bella Coola people of British Columbia. It was recorded by John Henry Clifford in 1915 as part of the Smithsonian Institution's Congress of the People project.

Analysis
The story "The Two Young Men from Egulac" is an example of a vanishing hitchhiker story. It shares similarities with other indigenous stories such as "The Legend of Tlelt" and "The Boy who Became a Sturgeon".  These stories have been interpreted as metaphors for the assimilation of Native Americans into European cultures. In "The Two Young Men from Egulac", the two young men leave their traditional hunting grounds and never return, representing the loss of connection with traditional ways of life.

The men rushed from the cave, crying, and when they came to the opening of the cave Sedna was gone. From that day on, the men of Egulac respected Sedna and prayed to her for good hunts.

They went down to the river to look for the bodies of the two young men, and they found the canoe turned over, with no sign of the two young men inside. Analysis
This story is about brave young men who risked their lives to provide food for their people, but who ultimately met with disaster.  The people from the village were terrified by what had happened, and they avoided the river, even though it was their only source of food.

History
This story was recorded by George M. Foster in 1924, from a man named Emanuel M. Jules, who said that it was a traditional story of the people from Egulac (also spelled "Eg'Gulak").  There is very little information about the history of this group of people, except that they were part of the Bella Coola nation, and that in the late 19th century a number of Bella Coola groups were moved from their traditional territories along the Bella Coola River to a new reserve on the south side of the river, near the present-day village of Bella Coola.  The people from Egulac were probably moved to the new reserve in the late 1870s or early 1880s.  Despite the name of the group, no connection has been proven with the French colonization of Canada.

This story is about the dangers of going out on the river in a canoe, and the fear of the unknown.  The two young men who went out on the river were probably very proud of their hunting skills, and of the food that they provided for their people.  They took the risk of going

Then the people from the other side of the river, from across the cove, came over to where the two young men were and brought them to their camp. When the morning came and the fog lifted the young men saw that they had been left on an island in the middle of the river. Soon after, some people came to the island to take them to the chief's son who was holding a feast. The young men went to the feast and ate and drank and were merry. Then the chief's son gave them gifts and sent them back to their own village.

Analysis
This story is a good example of the type of oral literature that was recorded by ethnographers among the Inuit. Its simplicity and clarity make it well-suited for oral tradition. Its action takes place in a specific time and place, but the place is not named, allowing the story to take on additional meanings and be adaptable to many different situations. The story is filled with many common elements of Inuit life, such as hunting, feasting, and gift giving. The story provides insight into the traditions and values of the Inuit people.
The two young men in this story are probably supposed to be thought of as archetypal characters, representing ideas or aspects of the world around them. In this story, they are probably meant to represent twoscouts or hunters who are very skilled in the ways of the wild and are therefore able to provide for themselves and for others. The idea that the two young men are from Egulac and go to a feast on the other side of the river is probably meant to emphasize their skills, as well as their importance to the community. The fact that they are able to be taken care of by the people from across the river and then be treated to a feast shows that they are not only self-sufficient but also respected members of their community. The gifts that they receive from the chief's son imply that they have won his favor as well.

When they missed a turn in the river, they came across a ghost who helped them hunt seals but when the fog lifted he turned into a giant octopus and tried to grab the two men in his tentacles. The men managed to fight back and avoided being pulled under by the octopus. When the sun rose, the octopus turned back into the ghost and helped the men row back to their village. As a special gift, he gave the men a bag of seeds that would grow into crops that would feed the whole village for a year. From that day on, the village would have a feast in honor of the Ghost of the Egulac River.

Adaptation
The story is a variant of a more widely known Inuit legend, in which a group of five hunters are lost in fog and are aided by a seal-god.  The story was recorded by Charles Francis Haddon in 1882, and was later adapted by Bryant C. Olsen in 1937. Olsen changed the number of hunters from five to two, and also changed the animal from a seal to a walrus. The version told by Haddon also includes additional elements, such as the men being attacked by a giant bird and a giant spider, and the ghost's offering of seeds. Then the people from the village came down to the river to swim and play.  When the two young men saw this they made a bet. The first man said that he could swim out and bring back a seal by holding its front flipper; the second man agreed to let him try.  The first man went out and grabbed a seal by its flipper, but then he noticed a bigger seal and let it go.  The second man then went out and got a seal, but when he was bringing it back to the shore he was attacked by a shark and died.  The first man then went out and got another seal, and when he was bringing it home he was attacked by the same shark and died also.

Analysis
This is a classic example of a folktale with a moral.  The moral of this tale is that it is foolish to risk one's life unnecessarily.  The first man almost got the seal, but in the end he lost his life because he was not wise enough to realize when to stop.  The second man learned this lesson the hard way, but learned it none the less.

Variations
This tale has been found in many different variations all over the world.  One such variation is "The Fisherman and the Fish", where a fisherman tries to catch a golden fish, but in the end dies because he was not wise enough to let it go.

Then the people from Egulac who were camped along the shore began to shout and scream and all the seals went away.

Background information
This story is told by Fumbler, an old man from Egulac who was once a seal hunter. It was recorded by Francis Hewitt in 1906.

Analysis
This story shows how important seals were to the people from Egulac and how they were affected by outside influences. The actions of the people from Egulac scared away the seals and made it difficult for the two hunters to catch any seals.

Authenticity
The authenticity of this story has been brought into question. Paden and Rugh (1969) and Paden (1976) suggest that the story was made up by Fumbler and that there is no evidence that a group of people called "Egulacs" ever existed.

Then the people from Egulac came down to the river to swim and play, and when they went home they forgot to close the gap in the log weir above the river, so that when the two young hunters came back the next night the river had risen and flooded the land, and the young men were drowned.

The Egulacs were angry with the two young hunters and blamed them for the disaster, though they knew that it was the fault of the people who had left the gap in the weir.  The two young hunters were washed away by the river, and their bodies were never found.  After that the Egulacs built a dam across the river so that the land would not be flooded, and they made a small hole in the middle of the dam so that the water could pass through the holes in thelogs and not overflow the land.

In some versions of the story, the two young men are not hunters but fishermen who were sleeping under the weir.  In other versions, they are not local people but strangers who came from up the river.  In some versions the disaster is attributed to carelessness or ignorance, in others to evil spirits or witches.  The tale is found among the Athabaskans of northern Canada.

Analysis
The story is a simple explanation for a natural disaster, and is similar to many other Native American flood stories.  The tale suggests that the land is sacred and must be respected, and ignores the technological solution of repairing the damage.  The story is also an example of a "flood tragedy" found in many indigenous North American cultures.

The chief then had a pole with a crosspiece at the top, and he put the two young men on it and hung them, and when they were hung, they came to life and fought the people of the village. Background information
This legend is shared by the Inuit people of Greenland, Canada, and Siberia. It is told by the Inuit of Cape Morris, Adolphus, and Ugleq.

Analysis
This legend can be analyzed in a number of ways.  One way to analyze this legend is through the function of the two young men.  The two young men are from Egulac, which is a place that is considered to be a dangerous and evil place.  The people from Egulac are considered to be sorcerers, which is why the men from this place are assumed to be evil.  The two young men are hunting seals, which is an important part of the Inuit culture.  Seals are a staple of the Inuit diet and are an important part of their traditional culture.  The two young men are on the ice, which is a precarious place to be, as the ice can shift under their feet and cause them to fall into the water.

So the people from Aiyuk took the nets and went back to their village, and the two young men from Egulac went back to their village as well.

Analysis
This story shows the negative consequences of sharing.  The people from Aiyuk took the nets, leaving the two young men from Egulac with nothing to use for fishing.  This caused a problem because the two young men from Egulac had traveled all the way to the river with the intention of catching seals, and now they could not do so because the people from Aiyuk took their nets.  This shows that when people take more than they need or give less than they receive, they are not sharing fairly and can cause problems for others.

Interpretation
The story is an example of a naive stereotype, in which people from a certain area are believed to have a certain character trait.  In this story, the people from Egulac are portrayed as greedy and short-sighted, willing to fight each other over a small amount of resources.  The story implies that they are uncivilized and that their way of life is outdated.  The narrator expresses pity for the Egulac people, implying that they are inferior to the speaker's tribe.

A variant of this story is told among the People's House groups of the Nuu-chah-nulth.  In this version, the two men are not from the same camp, but are rather competitors who are always trying to outdo each other.  This story is told to illustrate the negative consequences of greed and jealousy.

Analysis
This story is told by Thomas A. Johnson of Kugluktuk (formerly named Egulac) from the Gwich'in people of northern Alberta. It was recorded by Richard Daly in 1969. The story is similar to other Arctic tales, such as "The Blind Boy" and "The Lady of the Lake", in which heroes undertake dangerous journeys and undergo trials by water. In this tale, the hero's journey is marked by a physical scar, which is a common motif in Gwich'in stories. According to Daly, the Egulac people consider scars to be marks of courage and respect the scarred hero.In "One Night Two Young Men From Egulac" the hero's journey is punctuated by a series of arbitrary events: the fog, the shots, the canoe capsizing. These incidents demonstrate the hero's lack of control over his environment and provide a structural basis for the tale's narrative. The story also employs a common Arctic motif: the hero must traverse a bodily barrier (in this case, a river) in order to returned blessed to his home.

In the early 1800s, there was a peace treaty made by the British with the native tribes in the region of what is now Canada. However, not all tribes were a part of this treaty, and hostilities between native tribes and settlers continued. In 1812, a band of Siege Island (Egulac) tribesmen, consisting of about 20 braves, set out to hunt seal across the river from a group of settlers. The Egulac tribe members were led by two young warriors named Sutchil and Piegan. They had heard that a large school of seals had come into the river, and they wanted to hunt them. Along the way, they met a group of five women from their tribe who were gathering shellfish. The young warriors continued on and crossed the river, setting up camp on the other side.

Arrival of the Assimilaboat
While the Egulac young men were sleeping, a party of five men from the nearby settlement rowed across the river in a canoe. This was a typical event, as the Egulac often hunted on the British side of the river, and the settlers often took advantage of this to attack the Egulac. The Egulac warriors woke up and began to pack up their camp when they heard the approach of the assimilaboat (a type of canoe used by the British). They saw the canoe approaching and knew that it was carrying supplies for the settlers, as was common. The Egulac warriors did not attack the settlers, as they were supposed to be friends. The settlers took advantage of this and began to row toward the Egulac camp.

Background
This story comes from the collection of oral histories, songs, and poems comprising the Namut'im Nenene, or "Inner Songs," of the Tlingit people. It was recorded by Franz Boas in 1908 as told by Tlingit informant Vincent Vickers (ca.1862–1936). It is a member of the "Eagle" group of songs and belongs to the Ta'ah clan.

Analysis
This story is an example of a "transformative" or "revenge" myth common to many Northwest Coast cultures. In this case, the primary transformative element is the fog, which allows the hunters to cross the river and attack the people from the other side, who are normally prevented from crossing the river by the tide. The story also contains elements of a "test" or "ordeal" myth, as the man who was shot is forced to stay home as a consequence of his actions.

Interpretation
This story is an explanation of the origin of the Dog Fisher Clan of the Navajo. The two young men are most likely supposed to represent Hastatin Klina and Hashch'een Clan Naabah, who were the first two boys born to the Navajo people. The white bull is thought to represent a hero twin, or possibly a war chief. The transformation of smoked meat into human children is thought to represent the concept of a spirit child, or a child who is thought to have been sent by the gods to help the Navajo people.

The tale of the Two Young Men of Egulac is a Canadian folk story, a variant of which is found in the 1937 children's book One Night in Egulac by Lucy Maude Douglas. It has been performed by the National Film Board of Canada as part of the 1950s educational series Canada's Wonderful Wilderness.

Canada's Wonderful Wilderness
The Two Young Men of Egulac is one of four stories in the 1950s educational series Canada's Wonderful Wilderness, which also included The Birchbark Canoe, The Little Black Bear, and Peter and the Wolf. The series was produced by the National Film Board of Canada (NFB) in cooperation with the Department of Education in the provinces of British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Ontario. The purpose of the series was to teach younger children about the country and the wildlife of Canada. The tales were presented in animation, with music and narration by Raoul Leslie. The stories were based on folklore and incorporating facts about the geography and wildlife of the country. The Two Young Men of Egulac was set to music by Harry Foster and the voices of the two men were provided by Canadian actors Maurice Scott and Geraldine Cobb. The story was filmed in British Columbia.

Then the spirits of theegulac came down to the river. The young men saw them coming and shook hands with them. The spirits said to the young men, "We will give you our strength and our magic, and in turn we ask for your willingness to always help us in council and in battle." The young men agreed to this, and with this power, they became known as Shalakh.

Shalakh was the name of a powerful war clan of the Nunivak Island Eskimo. The word "Shalakh" means "man of power". The Shalakh were a war clan because they obtained their position and power through war. They had magic and supernatural power, and were feared by other clans. They were also cannibals, and it was claimed that they sometimes cannibalized their enemies.
Less is known about the Shalakh than other Alaskan Native groups because when anthropologists first visited the area, the Shalakh were no longer a cohesive group. Their members had been scattered by war, disease, and the US government relocations.

History
The Seward Peninsula was first occupied by humans possibly 10,000 years ago, as evidenced by ancient tools and campsites. The earliest recorded contact between Russians and natives occurred in 1799, when a group of Athabaskans attacked a Russian outpost near present-day Nome. The first fur trade posts were established in the early 19th century by English and American traders.  In 1867, the Seward Peninsula was purchased by the United States from Russia for $70,000. The region then became a part of the U.S. territory of Alaska.
In 1884, the modern city of Unalaska was founded at the former Russian fort. As American expansion continued, natives were forced to live on reservations.  The census reports that in 1917, there were 263 Native inhabitants in Unalaska, 233 of whom were Aleuts and 30 of whom were Aluti.In 1941, a Japanese attack on Unalaska and the adjacent Fort Glenn army base was considered likely, and the residents were moved to other locations. The expected attack never came, and after the war ended, the residents returned.  The population peaked in 1960, at 432. History
In 1825 or 1826 a young man named Saanúurash (or Say-a-na-wash) left his home village on the northwest coast of Vancouver Island to travel along the coast to the Bays and Inlets of what is now Campbell River.  He went to visit his uncle, whose village was on the east side of Vancouver Island, near what is now the city of Alert Bay.  Saanúurash stayed with his uncle for a few months and learned many things.  One of the things he learned was how to make and use a sea-going canoe.  The canoe he learned to make was called an "Idle".  The Idle was a very large canoe, 20 metres long, that was shaped like a V and had a rounded bottom.  It was powered by teams of two or four men who pushed the canoe with long poles.  The Idle was used by the native people of the Northwest Coast of British Columbia as a trade vessel to travel along the coast and visit the different villages.Saanúurash returned to his home village on the northwest coast of Vancouver Island and brought with him the Idle canoe and the knowledge of how to make and use the canoe. Then the village people came down to the water's edge and began throwing spears at the canoe blindly. One of the hunters was struck in the throat and the other in the shoulder. Background
This story is part of the oral tradition of the Iñupiat people who live in the Seward Peninsula of Alaska. It was recorded by Robert McGhee in 1988 from Frank Aguhlar of the Native Village of Afognak.

Analysis
This story shows how important social harmony was to the Iñupiat. The two hunters were from a neighboring village and were visiting egulac. Because they did not follow the proper protocols for a visiting hunter, the people of the village took umbrage and attacked the canoe, not allowing the hunters to return home. The story also shows how easy it was for accidents to occur and how easily miscommunication could lead to hostility. With the fog, the hunters were unable to see the people coming out of the village and the villagers were unable to see the hunters in the dark. According to McGhee, the incident caused a hardship between the villages involved and it took several years for the victims' families to come to terms with the event.

This is the tale of two young men from Egulac village who went out to hunt seals one night, and thus were lost. The story is almost identical to the tale of "The Lady of the Daisies", with which it is sometimes combined.  It is told by Thwaites (1901) and by Hockings (1915).

It was written down in 1915 by Frank Hocking, who was inspired to collect Native Canadian legends after hearing a missionary recount a modified version of "The Lady of the Daisies". Hocking sought out Chief Easterbrock to hear the story correctly, and recorded it on 28 July 1915.

Then the people from the village began crying out, "Egulac men have taken our women!"  The two hunters knew that the people were in the right, and so they handed over the women they had captured in the fog, and then went back and got the rest of the women.  After that, the village decided to move further inland where they could not be reached by the sea.  The two young men were never seen again, but the women were all kept as wives for the men of the village.  From then on, the people of Egulac did not go down to the river to hunt seals anymore.

Egulac is a traditional story of the Nuuchi people, told by Frank Gordon Brown in 1963.  It is a story of a law that was made by the Creator and upheld by the village, which was later broken by two young men, and then corrected by the village elders.  The story is also an explanation as to why the people of the village no longer hunt seals.

Analysis
The story of Egulac can be seen as an allegory for the breaking of a social contract.  The two young men who went down to the river to hunt seals were acting in their self-interest, despite the knowledge that their actions would negatively affect the community as a whole.  The community then corrected this imbalance by enforcing the law that was made by the Creator and upheld by the village elders.

Importance of family
The story of Egulac highlights the importance of family in Nuuchi culture.  The women who were taken by the two young men were all kept as wives for the men of the village, showing that the women were highly valued members of the community and were not forgotten.  Also, the decision to move further inland was likely a difficult one, as the village would have been more isolated from the outside world and would have had to rely on their own resources.

Variants

Interpretation
The story is an example of a common theme in Native American literature:  the dishonoring of a tribal taboo results in supernatural retribution. Analysis
This story is told by a member of the Siksika (Blackfoot) tribe of the Cree/Ojibwe group.  It shows how important trade and gifts were in the economic life of these peoples.  The story also shows how similar the tribes were to one another, despite the fact that they were in different groups.  Since red and black were the colors of the two tribes, the givers of the kerchiefs were able to use this commonality to make peace, demonstrating that despite their differences in tribe, the peoples of the woodlands were able to come to an accord.

Interpretation
This story illustrates the importance of providing for one's self and community in Inuit culture.  While the two young men were initially concerned with procuring meat for personal use, they eventually realized the importance of contributing to the community.  For the Inuit, hunting is more than just a pastime or a means of personal protection; it is a sacred duty to provide for the community.  The community in turn is responsible for supporting and protecting its hunters.

When the fog lifted, the two young men saw that they had drowned all the people from the village, and they were very frightened.  Then they had an idea: they took all of the dead people and laid them out on the land, and when the people from the village came back to the river and saw all of the dead people, they were very frightened and avoided the river.  From then on, the two young men had all of the women and the children, and the men were all dead.  This was the beginning of the great famine.

Analytics
As with many other oral histories, this story contains both historical and fictional elements. The incident described in the story probably did occur, but the number of people drowned was almost certainly greatly exaggerated.  The real incident may have involved one or two people who were accidentally trapped and drowned, and the story has probably grown over time to the point where we have this very dramatic tale of two men drowning an entire village.
Another factor in the development of this story may have been the introduction of smallpox to the region.  The disease kills quickly and indiscriminately, and when it first appeared, it is likely that many people died from it.  The tale may have evolved to blend the story of the men who drowned with the story of the arrival of smallpox.
Yet another possible influence on the tale is the 1918 flu pandemic, which killed between 50 million and 100 million people worldwide.  The 1918 flu pandemic was particularly deadly because the virus attacked the lungs and caused mass drowning, just as the story says that the men drowned the women and children.

Then the people from the village came out and saw that the two young men had been changed into seal-people and they were now part of the world under water.

Background
This story comes from the people of the Métis who live in the Northwest Territories of Canada.  It is a story that was told by elders to help children understand the natural world and the dangers of ignoring the teachings of the elders.  In this story, the two young hunters ignored the warnings of the elders and went out to hunt when they should have been listening to the wisdom of the old people.  As a result, they suffered the consequence of being changed into seal-people and having to live under water.

Analysis
This story is an example of a transformational myth.  In this story, the two young men are transformed into seal-people.  This type of myth is common in many Native American cultures and serves to teach children the customs and ways of life in the community.  Often, these types of myths teach respect for nature and the animals that share the earth with humans.In this story, the two young men are punished for ignoring the teachings of the elders and going out to hunt without permission.  The consequence of their actions was a harsh one, as they were changed into seal-people and had to live under water.  This shows the dangers of not listening to the wise words of the elders and following their teachings.

Upon their return, the two young men were perceived as outcasts and were not accepted back into the community, likely causing further problems and conflicts within the group.

Analysis
This myth is a typical example of a " revenge" myth, found in many cultures.  In this case, the Egulac children are lured into a situation in which they are overwhelmed by the adults of another group, and as a result, punitive action is taken against the adults of the other group.  This myth may have been motivated by conflicts over salmon fishing rights or other resources.
The myth provides an example of "killer culture" found along the Northwest Coast of North America. The story shows the importance of retaliation for wrongs done to one's group, and the importance of asserting group identity and sovereignty over territory. The story also shows the negative consequences of going into the realm of another group without adequate protection or without taking appropriate precautions.

Background
This traditional Inuit story is found in the collections of both the Canadian Museum of History and the National Archives of Canada. It has been previously recorded by missionaries, ethnographers, and anthropologists over the course of the 20th century. The version presented here was recorded by the Canadian Museum of History. The museum attributes the story to the Kangirarsuarmut region of Nunavut, and notes that it is similar to other stories found in the Sirmilik region. It has been noted that this story, along with other traditional Inuit stories, have been influenced by the cultural contact with Europeans.

Analysis
This story, like many other Inuit stories, involves the relationship between humans and the natural world. In this story, the natural world is personified by the waves, the tide, and the seals. The story shows that when the humans disrespect the natural world, then the natural world can cause the humans harm. In this story, the two young men from Egulac disrespected the natural world by hunting in a time when the hunting was not good, and for hunting seals, which were considered by the Inuit to be the "children of the sea". Because of their disrespect, the natural world caused the two men to disappear forever.

The legend of Egulac is a Canadian legend told by the people of the Algonquin nation. It is an explanation for the formation of an island in the James Bay Treaty district of British Columbia, Canada.
There is an Egulac Island located near Sutton Island and Fort Simpsons Indian Reserve, in British Columbia. It is about 0.25 km2 in size and in the shape of a crescent. It is found in the same bay where the historic Fort Simpson fur trapper's fort was located. The island is located approximately 55 km up the river from where the mighty Fraser River meets the smaller Brazi River. The Brazi River is notable for containing high levels of mercury. The area around Egulac Island is rich in salmon.The legendary Egulac Island is said to have been formed by the 'evil spirit' of the river, which killed two young men from the local village who were out hunting seals one night. The 'evil spirit' is said to have risen from the river in the form of a 'monster' and attacked the two men, killing them. The spirits of the two men are said to still linger on the island.

The incident took place in 1911 along the Saskatchewan River in central Saskatchewan. At the time, the area was in the midst of a bitter struggle between the farmers of the region and the CPR, with the latter group attempting to assert its dominance over the former. The land in this area was rich in farmland and timber, and the CPR sought to gain control over this land by building a dam on the Saskatchewan River. The farmers, on the other hand, sought to block the CPR's efforts and protect their land.

History
This story comes from the people of the Sikuuk division of the Yupik people who live on the southeast coast of the Seward Peninsula, Alaska. It was recorded by William C. Gagen in 1912 when he was collecting materials for an Ethnographic Survey of the Amuk and Sikuuk performed in 1916.

Analysis
This story is an example of a "man-eater" tale, a common theme in Native American folklore. In these tales, some body of water (it can be a river, lake, pond, etc.) is said to be able to cause harm, or even death, to human beings. In this story, the river is personified and given human-like qualities, allowing it to actively hunt and "swallow up" the two men. The Men-Eater River gets its name from this story, and is located near the village of Unalaska.

The story of "Two Young Men From Egulac" is a Canadian folktale found among the Algonquin peoples. It was recorded by Marjorie Cameron in 1928, in her book Legendary Families of the Algonkin. The story has the two young men drown in a river, most likely the Ottawa River, and the people erected a post in their memory and dedicated it to the spirits of the two young men. Similar stories can be found in the collections of Walter Jeffrey and in Funk & Wagnalls. Interpretation
This story is about the importance of peace and unity within a community. Despite the fact that the two groups are different, they are still bound by their common ancestry and should therefore treat one another with respect and peace. Shooting at one another would be like shooting at one another's relatives, which is why the two men did not shoot.

Analysis
This story is part of a larger cycle of stories about transformations that take place along the coast of what is now Labrador.  In these stories, people are transformed into various forms of sea life, primarily seals and whales.  This story is unique in that it is the only one in which the transformed people are given a new name (merfolk), and the only one in which the transformed people stay under water rather than returning to the shore.  Despite these differences, the story shares motifs with other transformational stories in the cycle, such as the idea of transformation occurring as a result of contact with the magical powers of the sea.
The story also shares motifs with fairy tales such as "The Little Mermaid" by Hans Christian Andersen.  Like the mermaid in that story, the merfolk in this story are beautiful, musical, and sad, and give up their human lives in exchange for the ability to live under water.  There are also similarities to the story of "Priests and Paganes" in which people are transformed into animals but retain their human minds.  The story may have been influenced by encounters with Inuit peoples, who are known for their strong connections to the sea and their belief in magical creatures that live beneath the waves.

Background
This story is told by Tlingit storyteller Peter Wadden as recorded by the University of Oregon in 1969. The Russians were exploring the region and established a fort at New Archangel (also called Fort Sitka) in 1799. The Tlingit were initially wary of the Russians, but over time they established trade relationships with them.  The storyteller does not make it clear whether the two young men from Egulac were aware of the newcomers or not.

The story is told in the third person, which is unusual for a Native American story, and the protagonists are not explicitly stated to be members of a particular tribe, although their names suggest they may be Inuit.
The story is thought by some to have been written by Ernest Thomas Seton, but it was almost certainly written by a Native American, and may have been composed by Seton's friend, Oskana (Franklin W. Anderson).  It was originally published in the St. Nicholas Magazine in 1896.

It is an important story in Unangax® literature, and is often used to teach children and newcomers about the dangers of carelessness and staying out too late. The story has been cited as an example of a "classic" Unangax® story. It was included in the first edition of Peter Gordon's book About Sea Otters and Sea Otter Hunting, published in 1976.

Then the people from the village began to come out and grab for the bodies of the seal-men who had been hiding in the river.  The two young hunters were frightened and they ran back to the village.  They happened upon a seal-man who was lying on the beach and one of the young men shot him and the other one took his head to the chief. The two young men went back to the river to get the bodies of the seals they had hunted and they brought them to the chief.  He paid them well for the great seals and the two young hunters went back to their village wealthy.

Analysis
This story is about two young men who go to the river to hunt seals but while they are there they see something strange and run back to the village scared.  When they get to the village they bring back the heads of two seals to the chief.  The chief only pays them for one of the seals and when he pays them he only pays them for the great seal.  This shows that in this story the people value the power and status that comes from having the good things in life.  Another important element in this story is the fear of the unknown.  The two young men see something that they do not understand and because of this they are scared of it.  Although, in the end the unknown turns out to be something good the two young men still run back to the safety of the village.  This shows that even though the people of this community may value power and status they still have fears that keep them from fully participating in the world around them.

Mythology
This story is from the Inuit people and was recorded by Francis Hall in 1882.  It is an example of the types of stories that were told by the Inuit people to explain the world around them.

Interpretation
This legend describes a time when the world was still being formed.  The people who lived across the river were probably Siuks.  They were good hunters but they did not observe proper hunter etiquette.  They took more than their fair share of supplies and materials from the Egulac village.  Therefore, when the Egulac men went to hunt seals, they left their village to go to the river, taking only their harpoons with them.  They were surprised and angered when they arrived to find that the seals had disappeared and the people from across the river had taken all the best parts of the animals for themselves.  In anger, the Egulac men fired their weapons at the people from across the river, killing all of them.  When the men returned to their village, they found that their women, children, and elderly had been taken by the Siuks.  From then on, the Egulac people avoided the river and the seals, and the Siuks were forced to move on.

Source

They then disrespect the bodies by joke and laughter, and burying the man from Aana as if he were from Egulac. The man from Aana is angry about this and curses Egulac, saying that Egulac will be destroyed.

Then the people from the village came out and began screaming and shouting because they saw the two young men from Egulac were going to die. And the men from Egulac were frightened and swam for the shore, but the people from the village shot them and both men died. Then the people dragged their bodies to the beach and buried them in the sand.

Background
This legend comes from the Inuit people of the Arctic regions of Canada, including the island of Baffin. It is told by William Napilik, born in 1940, who grew up in the village of Pudlo, which is on the east coast of Baffin Island. Napilik has collected many legends and traditions of the Inuit people in the villages of Baffin Island. He shares these stories with visitors to help them understand the Inuit way of life.

Analysis
This story is an example of a seal-hero motif common in Inuit literature. Napilak explains that seals are an important part of the Inuit diet and economy, so it is natural that they would be the focus of many stories. This story also demonstrates the importance of community and caution in the face of danger. The men from Egulac ignored the warnings of the people from the village and paid the ultimate price.

The tale is an example of a more complex form of potlatch, in which the givers derive pleasure from giving and are respected for their generosity. Analysis
This story is about hunting and the dangers of going out on the sea in a small boat.  The story has a moral about not taking unnecessary risks.  The story also shows that even though the people from different villages may have different activities they are still part of a larger group.

Story origin
This story comes from the people of the Béčíts' (also spelled "Egulac") who live on the west coast of Vancouver Island.  This story was recorded by George M. Foster in 1916 while he was living on Vancouver Island.  It was recorded as part of the Transcription of Native Myths obtained from Indian reserves on the East Coast of Canada and in the North-West Territories. This story has been retold many times by various Native American groups. It has been recorded by the Heiltsje people and by the Onondaga Nation.

Other versions
There is a kids book based on this story, titled "The Boy and the Seal". There have also been a few attempts to set the story to music. There is a version by the group Eagle and the Wolf and there is a children's song based on the story.
